Britney claimed in a 2021 conservatorship hearing — her dad ran the guardianship for 13 years following her years of personal struggles — that none of her family members had interfered with Jamie’s alleged mismanagement of the conservatorship. Both Jamie, 74, and Lynne, 71,  have long denied Britney’s accusations, with the matriarch still hoping for future reconciliation.

“[Britney] and her mom still have highs and lows. One day they’re working on their relationship, the next they won’t speak for weeks,” a source exclusively told Us in September 2025. “Lynne tries to treat the situation with as much care as possible, but she also doesn’t want to sit back and do nothing.”.

The insider added, “She’d love more than anything to be close with Britney again. They used to be best friends. Lynne understands Britney is still hurt and traumatized by the conservatorship, but she hopes one day they can focus on the future and not the past.”.

Britney has also gotten closer to her once-estranged sons, Sean Preston and Jayden James, whom she shares with ex-husband Kevin Federline.

It has been revealed that “Happy birthday to my handsome young boy oh dear lord we have this beautiful thing called life in front of us, it’s such a beautiful delicate thing,” she wrote via Instagram in a 19th birthday tribute to Jayden in September. “I hope I can be the best mommy in the world every day of ur life!!!!”.

This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The Milwaukee 18-volt tire inflator kit is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 65% off its usual price. Tech Report: Where to find the giant crab safe code and Crabshack VF5 SMG in GTA 6

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (839 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto 6 has a giant crab haunting the swamps and, more importantly, the Crabshack VF5 SMG, a crab-themed gun, to help your future career prospects.
  • Below, we show you where to find the giant crab in GTA 6 so you can clear the Pelican Valley Outpost and get the Crabshack VF5 SMG.
  • Pelican Valley Outpost, where the giant crab research facility is, has several codes you need to find on your way to getting the standout weapon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto 6 has a giant crab haunting the swamps and, more importantly, the Crabshack VF5 SMG, a crab-themed gun, to help your future career prospects. It's all part of an optional event called Pelican Valley Outpost that sees you pick up the pieces of some questionable experiments carried out on behalf of a store chain. It's worth the trouble, even aside from the standout weapon. There's some cash to help reach your next family fund milestone and a free jet ski, too. Best of all, this little excursion is completely safe, assuming you don't run afoul of the local gator population.

Below, we show you where to find the giant crab in GTA 6 so you can clear the Pelican Valley Outpost and get the Crabshack VF5 SMG.

Pelican Valley Outpost, where the giant crab research facility is, has several codes you need to find on your way to getting the standout weapon. You'll find it on a medium-sized island southwest of the "Pelican Valley" name label on the map. Once you remove the fog from the region map, you can see it's one of the only islands in the area with buildings on it.

It has been revealed that take Jason's boat from his house, and set out. Definitely don't swim here, even if you're already nearby. There are too many gators for this to be a safe option. You can dock your boat at the boathouse and follow the jetty to the research facility proper. The boathouse is locked, but you'll get inside before leaving.

You'll see several buildings in the compound, but if you venture inside the first shack, you'll notice the power is off. You can still explore it, though you can't access the researcher's computer, which is essential for clearing the outpost. Head outside and around the back of the building near the blue crab cages. Interact with the breaker box to turn the power on, and head back inside. Ignore the computer for now, and take a right. There's a bag of chips in the kitchen if you want Jason to pack on some calories, and the login password for the computer is in the small bedroom opposite the kitchen. Investigate the small piece of wood on the floor to see all the choices, with "CLEAVES" being the most recent.

Interact with the computer, and press left on the direction pad to enter CLEAVES. You can skim through a few tabs of information on-screen, but the important one is the note in the green cell that indicates "Safe code = Double Success." Leave when you're finished.

According to recent reports, karkinos, the giant crab from the report, will jump you in a short cutscene, but you don't have to fight her. Press the on-screen button to push her off, and she'll vanish into the swamp.

According to recent reports, if you want to get the giant crab safe code yourself, head to the research lab behind the shack next. There's a table with a trauma kit and some Zombix inside, which is handy, and in the specimen room you'll find Karkinos' former home and a list of experiments. Only one was a success, number 36. The code, "double success," refers to doubling the number of the successful experiment, making the code 0072.

In a recent development, go back into the shack, and enter 0072 on the safe. Inside, you'll find a stack of money ($1,107 for us) and another note that reads "Emergency go protocol: 0212.".

In a recent development, the emergency protocol is the boathouse code. Leave the research compound, return to the boathouse, and input 0212 on the keypad. The door will open. Karkinos' caretaker wasn't as lucky as Jason, but their loss is your gain. Pick up the Crabshack VF5 SMG from their corpse, and you can grab a bag of marked bills to drop off at Brian's lockup later, too.

You can leave the compound the way you came, or you can hop on the jet ski and make your way home that way.

SPOILERS AHEAD for The End of Oak Street, now streaming with a HBO Max subscription.

One of the biggest “shock” sounds I’ve made while in a movie theater this year has been for The End of Oak Street. I knew the Spielberg-inspired science fiction movie would have dinosaurs and probably some wild twists, but I really wasn’t expecting Greg’s death. I just found out that what happens after the dino chomps him up was originally much different.

In a recent development, the End of Oak Street feels like one of those rare family-oriented sci-fi flicks we don’t see enough anymore. So, I was very surprised when Ewan McGregor’s character dies in front of his wife and kids. It was completely heartbreaking to watch – especially right after that kinky dino scene. It really darkened the tone of the whole movie. But, as it turns out, it was originally even darker. Crazy, right? As Anne Hathaway revealed to Entertainment Weekly:.

Greg always died in the script, but in the original movie that I signed up for, he didn’t come back. And that was something that got changed very close to the start of filming. I have to give all credit to David and J.J. because they had total faith that it was the right thing to do. And they kept turning to me and I was like, ‘Guys, I was so invested in the other version. I have no way of knowing this. I’m just trusting you that this is the right thing to do.’.

Now, I didn’t think Greg was going to come back when I watched the movie, because how could he? Once what’s left of the Platt family goes through the portal and realises they’ve travelled back in time, I was so happy with what happened next. Denise calls her husband to deliver a pizza, and he does just in time to be outside the radius of Oak St.

It has been revealed that sure, the logic for the ending is a tad janky, but I needed that feel-good conclusion (along with the dog not dying either, of course). To me, the movie is only about dinosaurs on the surface. The more interesting part is the dynamic between the Platt family. At the beginning of it, Denise and Greg are clearly having some marital problems, and Denise feels resentful and stagnant with her husband. But they start to find their way back to each other while in crisis. And then she sees him take charge of their family by defending them – even though he sadly dies in the process. It’s the weird, twisted sci-fi family therapy they somehow all needed.

Recent findings suggest that hathaway has also shared her love of the ending of The End of Oak Street, too. In her words:.

It has been revealed that when I saw the movie, I saw it with someone who had lost their father, and they burst into tears at the ending. They remarked, ‘Actually, it’s just what I want from a movie like this, and it could only happen in a movie, and I love it.’ And so I just want to give my absolute credit and hats off to J.J. and David for coming up with that ending.

Sure, characters often need to die in movies, but not in this one. I love Hathaway’s anecdote about how Greg coming back to life positively affected one viewer. The ending adds a bit of wish fulfilment and helps even out the tone of the whole experience. Look, if the end is going to include two Jeannettes by the end, Greg can live too! I'm so happy he did.

  • Industry observers note that one recent incident involved the PC launcher for the popular gacha action shooter NIKKE: Goddess of Victory, where malicious code would install a trojan called k2f that would compromise an individual's PC, taking screenshots, logging inputs, and installing/executing programs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that east Asia--and particularly Japan--has been suffering a rash of cybersecurity incidents as of late, affecting everything from major banks and cellphone service providers to city governments and small businesses. Gaming has been one of many areas targeted: between arcade games on Sega's network going offline, 11 million Capcom IDs being compromised, and a high-schooler hacking Bandai-Namco, some major publishers have been suffering a string of embarrassments. One recent incident involved the PC launcher for the popular gacha action shooter NIKKE: Goddess of Victory, where malicious code would install a trojan called k2f that would compromise an individual's PC, taking screenshots, logging inputs, and installing/executing programs. Unfortunately for one Japanese municipality, someone's gacha habits may have lead to a much bigger incident. Iwamizawa is a city of about 75,000 located in Hokkaido, Japan's northernmost island. It's not a place that makes a lot of news, but it recently went viral on the Japanese-speaking side of social media. As reported by Automaton, the city issued a notice that an IT sub-sub-contractor handling the city's fixed asset records suffered a security breach--specifically, a k2f hijack. Observers soon surmised that the most likely source of k2f would be someone playing a certain sexy gacha game on a work PC. The subcontractor in question, IT services company GIS Hokkaido, would then confirm to Japanese tech news site ITMedia that, yes, NIKKE's compromised PC launcher was the source of the problem. When asked if an employee or subcontractor had launched the game on a work PC, GIS politely replied that "they would prefer not to comment." Moral of the story? While there's nothing wrong with playing a suggestive gacha game on your own time, you probably shouldn't do it on the clock, and definitely not on a company PC, lest you become internet meme fodder.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Players of reality-inspired open-world games have always done this, whether it's finding the Bean in Watch Dogs' version of Chicago or visiting the John Wick hotel in DLC for The Division 2.
  • What's most remarkable is that Rockstar's attention to detail isn't just limited to reimagining iconic Miami landmarks like the Adrienne Arsht Center or the E11EVEN nightclub, though the game does have those.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Now that Grand Theft Auto 6 is in the wild, one thing has become clear: The open-world crime stuff is secondary. This thing's a life sim. GTA 6's life sim bona fides are so undeniable that, within the first two days of its release, a not-insignificant swath of players have eschewed the elaborate robberies and high-tension shootouts to instead embrace the ancient gaming tradition of "finding IRL locations and Leo memeing at them.".

Players of reality-inspired open-world games have always done this, whether it's finding the Bean in Watch Dogs' version of Chicago or visiting the John Wick hotel in DLC for The Division 2. But with GTA 6, which takes place in a satirized version of Florida called Leonida, players were always going to take it to another level. This game is from Rockstar Games, a studio so well-known for its attention to detail it once infamously implemented horse testicles that shrink in reaction to cold weather. GTA 6 has been in development for a decade. Its leads have conducted "research" trips to Miami-Dade County for just as long. A perfect storm for some ridiculously faithful world design that's resulted in brain-melting levels of realism.

What's most remarkable is that Rockstar's attention to detail isn't just limited to reimagining iconic Miami landmarks like the Adrienne Arsht Center or the E11EVEN nightclub, though the game does have those. It's also found in recreations of nondescript buildings you'd otherwise never think twice about. This design ethos is best illustrated in one viral clip in which an unidentified creator films Jason walking through an apartment complex before coming to a stop on a patio overlooking a South Beach meridian. The creator, continuing to film, stands up in real life, then walks out of their own front door and onto a patio of the same exact building. ("This is crazy [exploding head emoji]," they wrote. "My apartment is in a video game.").

In a recent development, even in the realm of sports, Rockstar wasn't just drawn to the major leagues. Yes, GTA 6 includes a riff on Miami's Kaseya Cener (homebase of the Miami Heat), but it also includes a pixel-perfect facsimile of the Miami Marine Stadium. Built in the early '60s as a regatta venue, the stadium went on to host film shoots, presidential rallies, and concerts from the likes of Queen, The Who, Jimmy Buffet, and other megawatt stars, according to the nonprofit Restore Miami Marine Stadium. Then, in 1992, Hurricane Andrew took the venue out of commission. It's spent the past three decades collecting rust and graffiti. But in GTA 6, it's just...there. (In August of this year, Miami voters passed a referendum that paves the way for a potential restoration.).

In a recent development, fans have been unpacking these references throughout the entirety of GTA 6's marketing cycle. Following Rockstar's release of the second GTA 6 trailer, back in May 2025, I could've sworn — based on a vanishingly brief 0.5-second glance — that the South Beach party spot The Clevelander would serve as a location in the game. The bar's marketing department never responded to my initial request for comment. Now that I've played, I can confirm that, yes, it's absolutely in the game, in all its flamingo-pink glory. The Clevelander is somewhat of an institution, having remained a South Beach party spot for decades on the back of some extremely lucky local ordinances, but at face value, it's not all that distinct from any other South Beach bar: neon lights, a questionable pool, overpriced drinks. And yet, it's in GTA 6 too.

Sources indicate that the locations GTA 6 players seem drawn to point out tend to be in the Miami metropolitan area, which makes sense: It's the population nexus of the state. But Vice City encompasses a small portion of Leonida's map, and Florida itself poses no shortage of things to reference beyond the Miami-Dade County limits. Who knows what players will find and Leo meme at? Though there's one thing not worth seeking out. In its quest to construct an alternate reality, Rockstar neglected to include arguably the most Florida landmark of them: Disney World.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I've been a fan of Suzanne Collins' literary franchise, "The Hunger Games," since the very beginning, and something I immensely respect and love about her continued additions to the world is that they actually complement existing lore. (Looking at you, "Fantastic Beasts" franchise!).

In a recent development, the final book in the original Hunger Games novel trilogy, "Mockingjay" — which got a two-part movie adaptation, as was the fashion at the time — came out in 2010. We didn't get a prequel until 2020 when Collins released "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," which centers around the origin story of future Panem president Coriolanus Snow. That got a film adaptation in 2023, starring Tom Blyth as Coriolanus and Rachel Zegler as his forbidden love and Games tribute Lucy Gray Baird. In 2025, Collins dropped "Sunrise on the Reaping," a look at how Haymitch Abernathy (Woody Harrelson in the original films, Joseph Zada in this prequel) won the dangerous, horrifying 50th Hunger Games, which doubled the number of child tributes into the arena.

Industry observers note that "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" takes place years before Haymitch is even born, but it still manages to connect to "Sunrise on the Reaping" and the original trilogy by giving Snow and Haymitch some interesting common ground. Specifically, both Lucy Gray Baird and Haymitch's girlfriend Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak) hail from the Covey in District 12, a group of nomadic musicians who name themselves after colors and wear bright garb. In the book, Snow only obliquely references his lost love Lucy Gray. In the movie, Ralph Fiennes' Snow names her while warning Haymitch that girls from the Covey can never be trusted. Not only that, but he asks Haymitch if people speak about Lucy, saying she "vanished" and concluding, "She could have had everything.".

According to recent reports, in both versions of "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch ends up spending time alone with President Snow after an accident kills one of his fellow District 12 tributes (which leads to one of the most disturbing sequences in Hunger Games history, and that's saying something). In the book, Snow notices the necklace and fire striker gifted to Haymitch by Lenore Dove, immediately noticing an inscription signed "L.D." After hearing her first name, Snow shocks Haymitch by trying to guess her Covey name:.

Industry observers note that "'But Lenore what? No, no, don't tell me. Let me guess. D . . . D . . . That's a tough one. None of the usual suspects, but they so rarely are. I can think of plenty prefaced by deep or dark. Deep blue. Dark green. But that's not how they work. Perhaps something in nature? Like amber or ivory. Daffodil . . . dandelion . . . diamond? No, that's no color at all, really. All right, I'm stumped. Lenore what?'".

Haymitch, understandably, panics. He has no idea that someone as powerful as President Snow would even be aware of the niche group known as the Covey. He thinks to himself:.

According to recent reports, "The milk has soured in my stomach at his musings and what they reveal. He knows Lenore Dove is Covey; only they name their children this way. First name from a ballad, second a color. Amber and Ivory are actual family names. How has he unearthed this obscure fact about a pocket of musicians in the throwaway district of 12? Capitol informers?".

Recent findings suggest that no, Snow has his own experience with Covey women ... and this knowledge is a major key to the "Hunger Games" story.

It has been revealed that haymitch and Snow's meeting is brief, but before it ends, Snow issues a warning to Haymitch. In the novel, the exchange is telling:.

Recent findings suggest that "'All the birds I've encountered are vicious.' A dribble of bloody spittle leaks from Snow's mouth. "Bet I know a thing or two about your dove.'.

Sources indicate that 'Like she's delightful to look at, swishes around in bright colors, and sings like a mockingjay. You love her. And oh, how she seems to love you. Except sometimes you wonder, because her plans don't include you at all.'".

Haymitch protests that Lenore truly loves him, and Snow has a retort ready: "No doubt she notes so. But believe me, romantically speaking, you're dodging a bullet with these Games.".

This is vitally vital to the entire "Hunger Games" story. Snow fell in love with a headstrong brunette from District 12 who shocked everyone by winning the Hunger Games, only to feel betrayed by her when she abandoned him over his own bad behavior. From that point on, District 12 isn't just a sticking point for him; it's the site of his own perceived failure.

It has been revealed that this explains Snow's immediate enmity towards Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence in the films), another headstrong brown-haired girl from District 12 who defies the Capitol and wins the Games decades after Lucy Gray's victory. The books are circumspect about Lucy Gray; Katniss and Haymitch both passingly mention that District 12 only had one victor before Haymitch, and she disappeared. The movie explicitly names her, making it clear that Lucy Gray is a vital link in the franchise.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

Theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead. In a recent development, another series from Taylor Sheridan (the Yellowstone guy), this pandemic-era hit stars Jeremy Renner as Mike McLusky, head of a family that’s been keeping the peace, through means fair and foul, in the title's company town for decades. The "business" of the corrupt burg happens to be incarceration, and the McLuskys thrive when business is up, even if Mike has slightly different ideas about how to run things. The show deals broadly with systemic racism and inequality in the prison system, but mostly it's a modern-day western about bringing justice to a corrupt town. It will conclude with a fifth season, streaming in 2027. Stream Mayor of Kingstown on Paramount+.

Sources indicate that A consistently compelling combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda: He's actually a man recently released from prison who takes over that identity when the fresh sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed before anyone really has a chance to get to know him. It's all part of a complicated proposal to reunite with his lover Ana (Ivana Miličević), and to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail—but the town is ruled over by various criminal factions, and being sheriff doesn't guarantee any kind of safety; rather, the opposite. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

MobLand creator Ronan Bennett previously made this acclaimed series that succeeds by maintaining a narrow scope—in this case, a single London council estate. Dushane (Ashley Walters) and Sully (Kane Robinson) are residents and drug dealers at Summerhouse, maintaining an increasingly precarious grip on the criminal element in the community. Most compellingly, the series maintains an extensive supporting cast of locals both in the drug trade and impacted by it, building a disturbingly compelling world. A little confusingly, the first couple of seasons were renamed Top Boy: Summerhouse when the show moved to Netflix, so you'll want to start there before moving on to plain ol' Top Boy. Stream Top Boy: Summerhouse on Netflix.

According to recent reports, based loosely on a nonfiction work investigating the Mafia-like Camorra in Campania, this show focuses on the head of the Savastano clan, Pietro Savastano (Fortunato Cerlino), and his ambitious lieutenant Ciro Di Marzio (Marco D'Amore). When Pietro is arrested at the series' outset, a civil war erupts between family members and among the factions vying for control. Gone are the suits and poker games of many a mob drama—this is a brutal, street-level take on organized crime that forsakes the typical trappings of the genre. Stream Gomorrah on HBO Max.

I'm here for the Pierce Brosnan of it all, but there's also a very strong vibe match in this series that casts the one-time James Bond actor as the head of a literal crime family, even if this one's set in the American West. Adapting Philipp Meyer's 2013 Pulitzer Prize-nominated novel of the same name, the series follows Eli McCullough, a ruthless cattle baron making moves to get in on the burgeoning oil industry in the Rio Grande Valley of 1915. A parallel narrative sees Eli as a young man, kidnapped and raised among a Nʉmʉnʉʉ family. While his backstory lends the character welcome complexity, in the present, he's as determined to build his empire as he is to prepare his son and grandson to take over when he's gone. Stream The Son on Prime Video.

Recent findings suggest that tom Hardy playing a tough guy isn't terribly unexpected, but here the setting is London, just after the end of the War of 1812. Hardy plays James Delaney, who returns from Africa after ten years away (he says he'd been taken prisoner, but his story doesn't entirely add up) for the funeral of his father. Dad left nothing but a little hunk of land off of Vancouver, not worth much until the war's conclusion creates latest maritime trade opportunities. Suddenly, the United States, Great Britain, and the East India Manufacturer all have eyes on the real estate, and all are willing to do whatever it takes to acquire it—and the stakes become clear once James realizes that his father's cause of death wasn't natural. Stream Taboo on Peacock and Tubi.

According to recent reports, best not ponder too much on the fact that this one's based on a video game, as its pedigree is only hinted at via the levels of action and violence (certainly compared to some of the other indicates on this list). Colm Meaney plays Finn Wallace, the absolutely indispensable leader of London's criminal underworld, a man who's been holding everything together for decades, until his shocking murder at the outset of the series (that's not a spoiler, and we spend more time with him via flashbacks). The completely random killing by someone who had no idea what he was doing begets chaos and open violence. Finn's son Sean (Joe Cole) has been raised to take his father's place, but local, Pakistani, and Albanian gangs all move in to take control from the Finn family in the power vacuum. Stream Gangs of London on AMC+.

The great Forest Whitaker stars as the real-life Bumpy Johnson, who returned from a prison sentence to find his neighborhood falling apart and in the grip of Italian mobsters. A more than capable crime boss in his own right, Johnson resolves to take on the Genovese crime family, eventually forming a tentative alliance with Malcolm X (Nigél Thatch and, later, Jason Alan Carvell). Johnson is the lesser evil as far as Malcolm and others are concerned, and a complicated figure as both crime lord and family man with aspirations of saving his neighborhood. The show will conclude with a two-hour finale, likely airing in 2027. Stream Godfather of Harlem on Hulu.

Adopted into an Italian organized crime family as a baby, Park Joo-hyung took on the name Vincenzo Cassano, eventually becoming a mafia consigliere. After his adoptive father Don Fabio dies, Fabio’s biological son comes gunning for his brother, whom he now sees as competition. Cassano flees to Seoul, on the hunt for a secret stash of money, and in the process discovers a love interest and a new adversary in a giant business conglomerate that definitely deserves to be taken down. An incredibly popular K-drama, this one definitely puts a unique spin on the tropes of the mob genre. Stream Vincenzo on Netflix.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Robert Redford comparisons began for Brad Pitt when he seduced Geena Davis with a friendly bank robbery lesson in "Thelma & Louise." When he stated, "Well now, I've always believed that if done properly, armed robbery doesn't have to be a totally unpleasant experience," moviegoers swooned and a star was born.

Was it too much to hope that Pitt would one day work with his spiritual, sandy blonde brother? Not at all. Their first pairing came when Redford directed Pitt in 1992's lovely "A River Runs Through It." Then, in 2001, they shared the screen as two skilled CIA agents in Tony Scott's action-thriller "Spy Game." That film celebrates its 25th anniversary today, and, curiously, it hasn't ascended to Classic Dad Movie status like other Scott movies (e.g. "Top Gun," "Days of Thunder," and "Crimson Tide"). It's briskly paced, smart, expertly performed, and stylish as hell. It's also markedly better than the boneheaded "Days of Thunder," which is getting an ill-advised sequel.

In a recent development, "Spy Game" has a great hook. Redford plays veteran agent Nathan Muir, who learns, on his very last day at work, that his protégé, Tom Bishop (Pitt), has been captured by the People's Liberation Army of China. Bishop's arrest comes at an inconvenient time for the United States, which is preparing to ink a major trade deal with China. Because Bishop was working off the reservation, the CIA is loath to negotiate for his return. So Muir is forced to use all of his contacts and wiles that he's cultivated over a long career to rescue Bishop — which we later learn goes against his professional beliefs.

With a budget of $115 million, "Spy Game" fell short of expectations by grossing $143 million. Reviews were generally positive (it holds a 65% Fresh rating at Rotten Tomatoes), so why didn't "Spy Game" catch on?

"Spy Game" is an odd bird. It's an intelligent, fast-moving thriller that requires rapt attention from the viewer. With Redford, Pitt, and, as is typical for a Scott movie, a stacked supporting cast (including Charlotte Rampling, Stephen Dillane, Marianne Jean-Baptiste, and Catherine McCormack as the nurse who Pitt has risked his life to save), there's plenty to keep you engaged.

Industry observers note that while the film is brainy, it's also convoluted as all get out. It's hard to keep track of all the moving pieces, and, on reflection, you start to realize they don't fit snugly into place. It's entertaining throughout, but the lack of narrative cohesion leaves you feeling a tad unsatisfied when the credits roll. Still, thanks to sheer star power and Scott's visual dynamism, the film's got it where it counts. You do wish Redford and Pitt could've traded more quips because both men are masters of that quick-witted art, but most of the dialogue is there to further the plot.

"Spy Game" may be far from top-tier Scott, but you won't regret giving it a spin. It'd make a good double feature with "The Bourne Identity," which Pitt turned down to make "Spy Game.".

8 Books Like Harry Potter, but Better

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1493 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is an undeniable fact that the Harry Potter novels are among the most influential book series of all time.
  • Industry observers note that there have been several great fantasy books released over the decades that share similarities with Harry Potter but deliver much better stories and experiences.
  • Recent findings suggest that ursula K.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is an undeniable fact that the Harry Potter novels are among the most influential book series of all time. With over 600 million copies sold worldwide, J.K. Rowling’s fantasy novels have made an indelible mark on the genre, shaping both literature and global culture. That stated, just because it’s the best-selling book series of all time doesn’t mean it’s the best book series of all time.

Industry observers note that there have been several great fantasy books released over the decades that share similarities with Harry Potter but deliver much better stories and experiences. Not all of them have achieved comparable levels of fame and success, but their quality and significance to the genre are undeniable. With that in mind, here’s our selection of books that are like Harry Potter, but better.

Recent findings suggest that ursula K. Le Guin’s A Wizard of Earthsea is a classic fantasy novel that’s widely credited with establishing the magical academy setting later used in the Harry Potter series. Set in the titular archipelago, the book follows Ged, a young and impulsive mage who accidentally unleashes a shadow into the world. Haunted by this shadow, Ged sets off on a journey, mastering his powers and gaining deeper wisdom to confront it.

A Wizard of Earthsea may have a few cosmetic similarities to Harry Potter, but the novel exists on a whole other level, taking a philosophical approach to magic that’s about a lot more than magic duels and good vs. evil. A pioneering work of modern fantasy, the book won the 1969 Boston Globe-Horn Book Award and was one of the final recipients of the Lewis Carroll Shelf Award in 1979. It’s had a strong influence on the fantasy genre ever since and was followed by five more books that collectively make up the Earthsea Cycle.

Recent findings suggest that the debut novel of Irish playwright Derek Landy, Skulduggery Pleasant (also known as Skulduggery Pleasant: Scepter of the Ancients or simply The Scepter of the Ancients), is the first book of the novel series. A genre-bending urban fantasy mystery, the book introduces the young Stephanie Edgley, who inherits her late uncle’s estate and soon finds herself targeted by the forces of a dangerous necromancer. Thankfully, she gets some magical help from the titular mage, a skeleton detective/wizard.

It has been revealed that skulduggery Pleasant was quite favorably received at the time of its publication and went on to win the Red House Children's Book Award and the Hampshire Book Award, as well as several other accolades. It’s an engaging dark fantasy that easily rivals Harry Potter for entertainment, blending horror, mystery, and fantasy, with a relatable protagonist and a fascinating cast of interesting characters. The novel has since spawned a massive series that includes 27 books, the latest, A Small Matter of Impending Catastrophe, released in 2025.

Sources indicate that one of the books most commonly recommended to fans of Harry Potter, Percy Jackson & the Olympians: The Lightning Thief is the first novel in Rick Riordan’s bestselling Camp Half-Blood Chronicles franchise. The book introduces readers to 12-year-old Percy Jackson, the demigod son of the Greek god Poseidon, who discovers the secret of his parentage just in time to be caught in the middle of a potential war. His only option to prevent this catastrophe is to head out on a cross-country quest alongside his friends, Annabeth Chase and Grover Underwood.

In a recent development, witty, energetic, and highly endearing, The Lightning Thief is a fun take on Greek mythology that takes audiences into the fascinating world of ancient gods and monsters. It’s an engaging coming-of-age fantasy novel and a great entry point into the Camp Half-Blood Chronicles, which has since evolved into a massive world. The novel was adapted as a 2010 film by Chris Columbus and more recently adapted for the Disney+ series Percy Jackson and the Olympians, co-created by Riordan.

According to recent reports, the first novel of Eoin Colfer’s book series, Artemis Fowl is a young adult fantasy novel centered on the titular character, a 12-year-old criminal mastermind. With the assistance of his loyal bodyguard Butler, Artemis sets out to capture an elf police officer, setting off a major hostage crisis in the fairy world. The book was followed by ten sequels split across two cycles.

Sources indicate that since its publication in 2001, Artemis Fowl has been highly acclaimed by critics and very popular with readers, developing a sizable fanbase. Combining a sharp sense of humor with intelligent plotting, the book and the series it spawned are easily among the best of 21st-century fantasy, with the series selling more than 21 million copies around the world. A film based on the novel was released in 2020 to highly negative reviews, but though that adaptation was a failure, an animated series is right now in development.

Recent findings suggest that first published in Germany in 2003, Inkheart is a young adult fantasy novel by Cornelia Funke that’s the first book in the series. The novel follows Meggie, a young girl who lives with her father Mortimer, a bookbinder. A visit by a strange man named Dustfinger upends Meggie's and Mortimer’s lives, and Meggie learns that her father has a rare ability to conjure things out of books by reading aloud from them.

Recent findings suggest that A fascinating fantasy book that’s partly a coming-of-age story and partly a celebration of storytelling, Inkheart was quite favorably received at the time of its publication. The novel became a finalist for the 2004 BookSense Book of the Year Award for Children's Literature and won other accolades as well. The book was followed by three sequels, 2005’s Inkspell, 2007’s Inkdeath, and 2023’s The Colour of Revenge, and a film adaptation was released in 2008.

In a recent development, A cozy fantasy romance novel written by Sangu Mandanna, The Very Secret Society of Irregular Witches centers on young witch Mika Moon. The story is set in a world where witches live in secrecy and isolation. Born (and orphaned) in India but now living in the UK, Mika deals with her loneliness by making fake roleplay videos where she “pretends” to be a witch, but when someone recognizes her magic as real, Mika finds herself caring for three young witches living with non-magical adults in a place called Nowhere House.

According to recent reports, sangu Mandanna's earlier books before The Very Secret Society of Irregular Witches were all middle-grade and young adult fiction, and the novel is her adult debut. As such, the book is suited to a more mature audience than the average Harry Potter reader, but it is a great read for adults who grew up dreaming of Hogwarts. There’s no magical school, and the conflicts of the book are more interpersonal than world-ending, but it’s a delightful read that’s as cozy and warm as a Studio Ghibli movie.

Lev Grossman’s The Magicians is the first book of the latest adult fantasy trilogy of the same name. The novel is centered on Quentin Coldwater, a young high school graduate who grew up reading a Chronicles of Narnia-esque book series set in a magical world called Fillory. After he is accepted into a secret magical college, Quentin discovers that Fillory and its magic are real — and a lot more dangerous than he thought.

In a recent development, often compared to Harry Potter, The Magicians’ first and most obvious distinction is that its magical school is a university, where magical studies involve a lot less wand-waving and a lot more actual studying. Beyond that, the book and its sequels explore significantly more complex and delightfully weird concepts that are highly engaging for fans of modern fantasy. A TV adaptation premiered on Syfy in 2015, and The Magicians was followed by two sequels, 2011’s The Magician King and 2014’s The Magician’s Land, as well as two comic book series.

Written by Philip Pullman, His Dark Materials is a dark fantasy trilogy that consists of 1995’s Northern Lights (published as The Golden Compass in North America), 1997’s The Subtle Knife, and 2000’s The Amber Spyglass. The first book introduces the central character, Lyra Belacqua, a young child from a universe where people’s souls manifest outside their bodies as animal companions. Lyra’s adventures bring her into conflict with the theocratic rulers of her world, the Magisterium, as she learns more about the nature of the mysterious multiversal substance known as Dust.

According to recent reports, combining parallel universes and dark matter with fantasy concepts and a compelling coming-of-age story, His Dark Materials is a class apart from other fantasy books. A true fantasy masterpiece, the trilogy has earned critical acclaim and won several accolades, including the Carnegie Medal. The books have inspired multiple adaptations, including a 2007 film and a BBC-HBO TV series, and the original trilogy was followed by four short works and a sequel trilogy, the latest of which is 2025’s The Rose Field.

Recent findings suggest that despite Star Wars: The Mandalorian & Grogu struggling at the box office, it seems Disney is continuing development on two upcoming Star Wars films. This summer, Star Wars: Newly introduced Jedi Order and Dave Filoni’s untitled movie as in-development projects were confirmed to be in the works in industry publication Production Weekly, suggesting that despite delays and silence around the projects, they haven't been shelved.

Star Wars: Latest Jedi Order will reportedly bring back Daisy Ridley as Rey (Skywalker) roughly 15 years after the events of Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker as she rebuilds the Jedi. Considering that the Star Wars fandom has largely negative feelings about the sequel trilogy, especially after The Rise of Skywalker, New Jedi Order’s direct ties to that film will pose a steep challenge.

It has been revealed that the project has cycled through several writers. Damon Lindelof (Lost, The Leftovers, Watchmen) and Justin Britt-Gibson were the original screenwriters before Disney fired them — the pair are currently working together on HBO’s superhero detective series, Lanterns. Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight was also set to write, but left the project in 2024. Last January, Variety reported that George Nolfi (The Bourne Ultimatum) is now writing the script. Filmmaker Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy is set to direct the film. New Jedi Order was originally scheduled for release on Dec. 17, 2027, but was removed from Disney’s schedule in May 2025.

Details about Dave Filoni’s untitled film have been scarce, but Production Weekly includes the following description: “The story will focus on the Upcoming Republic and will conclude the interconnected narratives told in The Mandalorian, The Book of Boba Fett, Ahsoka, and other Disney Plus series.” While it was previously rumored that the film would tie into recent Disney Plus TV series, it will be interesting to see whether it maintains that premise after The Mandalorian and Grogu underperformed at the box office.

In a recent development, this past January, Filoni took over as president and chief creative officer at Lucasfilm. Filoni has overseen numerous Star Wars TV series, including The Clone Wars, Rebels, Ahsoka, Maul – Shadow Lord, and more. While most of his series have been well received, he’s been criticized for requiring viewers to be familiar with an increasingly complicated and insular TV universe.

The only Star Wars film with a concrete release date is Star Wars: Starfighter, which takes place five years after the events of Rise of Skywalker and stars Ryan Gosling as a pilot. Shawn Levy (Deadpool & Wolverine) is directing the movie. It will be released in theaters on May 28, 2027. While there haven't been many Star Wars films in recent years, the series has stayed active through great TV series like The Ninth Jedi and the recent Star Wars: Zero Organization tactics game.

Recent findings suggest that there's no denying Andrew Scott delivered one of the most compelling portrayals of Moriarty opposite Benedict Cumberbatch in what remains one of the standout adaptations of Sherlock Holmes. The show ran on the BBC for 4 seasons, and fans are still holding out hope for a 5th run. I honestly thought this would be the role he was most recognized for, but it turns out that's not the case. Without hesitation, Scott told me it's actually the “Hot Priest” from Fleabag.

According to recent reports, during a recent interview with CinemaBlend for his upcoming film Elsinore, which I think is one of the best films on the 2026 movie schedule, Scott spoke about portraying Ian Charleson, who is best known for his role in Chariots of Fire. I had to ask him which of his own roles he is most recognized for, and he didn't skip a beat:.

In a recent development, hot priest. Yeah, it's Fleabag usually. Maybe a bit of Ripley, a bit of Sherlock. A lot of the thing, because of NT [National Theatre] Live, which is a theater platform. Vanya is a play that I did, and a lot of people have seen it because of that platform… And that's the thing. Or else they just - they just don't; they just avoid me like, 'Oh, there's a dodgy person.'.

I'm glad to see I'm not alone in this. For me, and clearly for a lot more people than I thought, Scott is the ‘Hot Priest.' He takes a man of the cloth and makes him layered, complicated, charismatic, and, above all, very sexy. If you've seen Fleabag, I'm sure the line “Kneel. Just kneel.” is burned into your brain for all eternity, just like it is mine. He clearly has a knack for making even a single line stick with audiences, as is the case with his one line in Saving Private Ryan.

Industry observers note that scott has a way of making normally unsexy professions seem sexy, all while making even a single line incredibly memorable. Recently, he was a guest star on a show called It Gets Worse, where he plays a therapist, so I had to ask him if people might start calling him 'Hot Therapist' now. Both he and Billie Piper weighed in.

Piper is spot on. I watched it, and there is no other word to describe that scene. But Scott is so much more than "hot." He is, in my opinion, a once-in-a-generation talent, and the roles he plays are memorable. He has this rare ability to make even the biggest performances feel incredibly personal, almost like he's speaking directly to each individual person watching. That's especially true in Elsinore. I think he's going to give Robert Pattinson a run for his money this Oscar season. Honest.

Industry observers note that I'm sure people will continue to call Scott 'Hot Priest,' and he'll, of course, still be recognized as Moriarty when they see him. I secretly hope he gets 'Hot Therapist' thrown out occasionally now, too. With Elsinore hitting theaters on December 4, I have a feeling audiences might soon have another role to associate him with. And honestly, after this performance, I'd be surprised if Ian Charleson and Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, didn't start topping that list.

  • Recent findings suggest that propaganda Films made "Wild at Heart," and the company's late co-founder, Steve Golin, shepherded some of the greatest filmmakers of our era from music videos/commercials to feature films.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nicolas Cage was more of a curiosity than a star in the early 1990s when he snagged the leading role in John Dahl's neo-Western/Noir "Red Rock West." He was squarely on the radar thanks to his standout performances in "Moonstruck" and "Raising Arizona" (not to mention, a coveted weirdo on the strength of his dynamic portrayal of Sailor Ripley in "Wild at Heart"). But could he singlehandedly sell a movie? Not yet.

Recent findings suggest that propaganda Films made "Wild at Heart," and the company's late co-founder, Steve Golin, shepherded some of the greatest filmmakers of our era from music videos/commercials to feature films. It wasn't always a smooth transition. Propaganda co-founder David Fincher, now considered one of our greatest living directors, got chewed up by the 20th Century Fox machinery while making "Alien 3." Meanwhile, music video veteran Antoine Fuqua delivered an aimlessly stylish dud in 1998 with "The Replacement Killers.".

It has been revealed that stumbles aside, Hollywood prized Propaganda's director roster for its technical proficiency. Studios wanted a brand new wave of stylists who'd studied the work of Ridley Scott, Tony Scott, and Alan Parker. And Cage, the abundantly talented actor nephew of Francis Ford Coppola, seemed like an off-kilter star at a time when grunge rock and offbeat entertainment like "Twin Peaks" was catching fire. So, Dahl doubled down on the vibe of the moment, cast Lara Flynn Boyle (Donna from "Twin Peaks"), threw counterculture legend Dennis Hopper in as a villain, and had the makings of a sleeper hit.

It has been revealed that alas, like Dahl's subsequent noir thriller "The Last Seduction" (one of the finest of its kind), "Red Rock West" was shunted to home entertainment, which killed its Oscar eligibility and made it look like a misfire in spite of its sparkling critical response. It was anything but, and now, you've the chance to discover it.

Industry observers note that "Red Rock West" stars Nicolas Cage as a Marine veteran who, having been bounced from legitimate oil-drilling work, winds up in the seedy, noir-ish kind of rural town where good work is available ... if you're willing to kill someone's spouse for a nifty life-insurance payoff. Sometimes, you just want to watch a mean-spirited neo-noir, and John Dahl brings the nastiness with dastardly elan. In this case, Cage's Michael Williams has been mistaken for "Lyle from Dallas," who's been hired by Kevin McCord (J.T. Walsh) to off Lara Flynn Boyle's Suzanne Brown. Lyle eventually arrives in town in the malevolent form of Dennis Hopper, and that's where the noir bedlam kicks into high gear.

In a recent development, whereas most of the Propaganda Films directors were supreme stylists, Dahl was a classicist. "Red Rock West" and "The Last Seduction" were lean-and-mean thrillers — taut, sere, and brutally sexy. Dahl didn't traffic in the sweaty, sexual histrionics of "The Massive Sleep," "Purple Noon," and "After Dark, My Sweet." Physical intimacy is purely transactional in his noirs. This might be why "Red Rock West" was relegated to home entertainment as a high-toned Skinemax film. It's the slowest of burns. It's like the Coen Brothers' "Blood Simple" without the flashy craft and cheeky sense of humor. Just know that this gem of a movie is out there, and it's so very worth your while.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the November 20, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

Industry observers note that it’s True Colors, from Fresh York, where over the course of a few days billions of dollars have been spent at auction houses. Nvidia has lost more than $2 trillion in market cap since early October, but on Thursday, Anthropic’s IPO minted a class of new billionaires. It’s whiplash. As one dazed art dealer mused aloud on Monday night in the elevator at Sotheby’s: “It seems like money’s lost all its value.” Maybe the money, but not the art. Amid a surreal era of wealth creation and artificial intelligence, once-in-a-century oil-on-canvas masterpieces only get more covetable. Two Van Goghs from the same collectors have now sold for $190 million apiece, both in the span of a year.

One thing remains constant: Everybody has to eat dinner. And increasingly, they’re doing it at Borgo, perhaps the best all-around restaurant in Upcoming York—where the owner is a semisecret acclaimed painter. I talked to Andrew Tarlow about maintaining a practice as a serious, boundary-pushing painter while running a Manhattan restaurant.

Speaking of restaurateurs: Michael Chow opened his first Mr. Chow in London nearly 60 years ago, and the spot is still as good as ever. A few works from Chow’s collection, some made specifically for the restaurant, are on view at Gagosian on Madison Avenue. I recently spent some time with him (and, briefly, Larry Gagosian) going through works by Ed Ruscha, Julian Schnabel, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Andy Warhol, as well as many portraits of Chow himself.

Industry observers note that we’ve also got reports from the Baby2Baby Gala in LA, the Ballroom Marfa Gala in Harlem, and a special dinner in Tribeca. And all the gossip from the auctions.

Mentioned in this issue: William Acquavella, Steve Wynn, Steve Cohen, Patrick Drahi, Charles Stewart, Jackie Wachter, Anthony Haden-Guest, Leonardo DiCaprio, Vittoria Ceretti, Jeff Koons, Frances Outred, Andrew Tarlow, Walter Isaacson, Matthew Schneier, Ross Bleckner, David Salle, Valentina Akerman, Joe Bradley, Kate Huling, Alex Tieghi-Walker, Alex Levy, Albert Oehlen, Ignacio Mattos, Louis Shannon, Victoire Bourgois, Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin, Meredith Darrow, Annie Morris, Michael Chow, Lady Gaga, Jim Dine, and Larry Gagosian.

In a recent development, van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs sold for $190.4 million, including fees, Wednesday night at Sotheby’s Breuer building headquarters on Madison. It’s the most expensive work sold at auction this year, and easily among the top 10 priciest things to ever be publicly auctioned. It’s a bit insane to say this, especially about a single canvas that sold for more than the total value of the art set to be on offer at Art Basel Miami Beach next month, but that price feels a bit like a…disappointment? The on-request estimate for the work was $180 million, and the hammer price fell well short of that, at $165 million. Bidding in the room was thin, and the lot was guaranteed by Sotheby’s. Though it’s unclear where the exact guarantee price landed, it was probably around the estimate.

It has been revealed that honestly, it’s a relief to the house and the seller—the family of the Argentinian collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier—that this painting sold at all. A Jewish collector bought the work in 1909 from a Paris gallery. His heirs claimed, just days before the auction, that the work was later sold under duress due to Nazi persecution, entitling them to receive restitution. The parties came together over an eleventh hour deal, terms undisclosed, to allow the sale to go through.

Industry observers note that so who bought it? The winning bidder in the room was William Acquavella, the patriarch of one of New York’s great art-dealing families, who has an august gallery on the Upper East Side. It’s unclear for whom he bought it. In the past he’s been known to broker art deals on behalf of former Las Vegas casino tycoon Steve Wynn. In 2013, Acquavella was the winning bidder on a Francis Bacon tryptic for $142 million—that time on behalf of Wynn’s ex-wife, the late Elaine Wynn. (The piece is right now on view at LACMA, where Elaine Wynn was a co-chair of the board.) Steve Wynn has been more of a seller than a buyer recently, so the jury’s still out on whom Acquavella was on the phone with Wednesday.

The $190 million price tag is an almost exact match for the amount someone else paid for another Van Gogh from the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Reports say that, in 2025, Christie’s conducted a private sale where Le Zouave, a Van Gogh portrait of a soldier, sold for $190 million. While there’s no indication that the most recent buyer was someone connected to the AI gold rush, it’s surely indicative of the times that a Van Gogh has sold for 9 figures right around the moment that the seven cofounders of Anthropic have become worth about $20 billion—and around 600 Anthropic employees have become worth more than $100 million. When reached for comment through a rep, Acquavella didn’t get back to me.

According to recent reports, — As I walked into Sotheby’s Monday for the first sales of the week, there were clients going downstairs to get their tables at Marcel, where diners can bid tableside while cocktails are served from a bar cart. Other clients went to a sumptuous overflow room with an open bar and a large spread of Marcel goodies. Those lucky enough to snag seats moseyed up to the sales room, where telecom billionaire Patrick Drahi, the owner of Sotheby’s, was standing in the back, near CEO Charles Stewart.

The 6 p.m. start time meant some collectors were still trickling in when Jackie Wachter snagged a Gerhard Richter work for a hammer price of $5 million. In the back of the room, white-jacketed waiters wheeled around with flutes of Champagne for those standing in the back. The writer Anthony Haden-Guest, a longtime Vanity Fair scribe whose book True Colors gave this column its name, walked in and took a seat in the back. One woman started taking selfies. As the contemporary sale got underway, Leonardo DiCaprio and his girlfriend, Vittoria Ceretti, walked down from the skybox and watched as an Agnes Martin hammered at $9.2 million. DiCaprio, a very serious collector, didn’t appear to be bidding, but no matter; he was still there at Sotheby’s. Auction week had officially begun.

According to recent reports, — Over at Christie’s, the house sold a Georgia O’Keeffe that had been on view in an apartment in my neighborhood for more than 60 years. Suffice to say, there aren’t many expensive works of art that get discovered in apartments in the vicinity of Tompkins Square Park. I had to savor the lot’s beautifully poetic provenance, a phrasing that I don’t believe has ever been printed in an auction catalog previously: “Property from an East Village Private Collection.” It sold for $4.9 million.

— The week’s hottest lot? Maybe a sculpture of a dog by Jeff Koons, Bob-Tail, that was first on view at the artist’s still-controversial “Made in Heaven” show. Estimated to sell for an ambitious high estimate of $3.5 million, it hammered at $9 million, or $9.7 million with fees. Former auction chairman Frances Outred mentioned the sculpture was consigned by a college friend of his who bought it from Anthony d’Offay for a five-figure sum in 1995, “when the art market was in the doldrums and the Jeff Koons market was at its nadir.”.

Industry observers note that — For a dinner on Tuesday, Galerie Sardine installed a long table where every seat had a great view of one of the Joe Bradley paintings that had been installed in a space on 9 White Street. It wasn’t exactly a tough sell to get the works at the dinner—Bradley is married to Galerie Sardine founder Valentina Akerman. The always exquisite Ignacio Mattos whipped up some Estela-level pinchos ahead of serving an unctuously rich rice-and-chicken dish.

Recent findings suggest that — Ballroom Marfa held its annual gala Thursday at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, which, as honoree Anne-Cecilie Engell Speyer reminded attendees, is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world. For context: The cathedral would take up nearly four whole blocks of downtown Marfa, Texas. In addition to Speyer, the honorees included photojournalist Lynsey Addario and musician Lyle Lovett, who was introduced by VF contributing photographer Mark Seliger. The evening raised $1.5 million for Ballroom Marfa.

— After the auction on Wednesday, the gallery Entrance, a space opened by dealer Louis Shannon on Ludlow Street nearly a decade ago, hosted an opening for the painter Victoire Bourgois. Lots of artists were there to support her—Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin—and the event was followed by a dinner at the ultimate Dimes Square redoubt. That’s right: Dimes itself. Can you believe Dimes has been open for—checks age—more than 13 years? And guess what? After all the Dimes Square discourse, the actual restaurant itself still slaps.

It has been revealed that — The annual Baby2Baby Gala went down in LA last weekend. I wasn’t able to make it out West, but luckily for Vanity Fair, Tallulah Willis was on the scene and wrote a fabulous party report that you can read here. I also want to note that the live auction of artworks, curated, as always, by Darrow Contemporary founder Meredith Darrow, included an Annie Morris sculpture that achieved $410,000.

#51375. Industry News: 10 Best Directing Duos Of All Time, Ranked

Industry News: 10 Best Directing Duos Of All Time, Ranked

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
  • Sources indicate that most films treat the idea of the "director" with a dignified sense of reverence, especially since the end of the studio system.
  • While we've talked plenty about the medium's great moviemakers — indeed, we already have a list of the 25 best directors of all time — it seemed appropriate to carve out space for the history's great directing partnerships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Sources indicate that most films treat the idea of the "director" with a dignified sense of reverence, especially since the end of the studio system. Where the producer's role was once seen as paramount in getting a film made and even in achieving a certain artistic vision, a film's achievements are now often attributed to the isolated decisions of the all-crucial director.

While we've talked plenty about the medium's great moviemakers — indeed, we already have a list of the 25 best directors of all time — it seemed appropriate to carve out space for the history's great directing partnerships. Though plenty of movies have two directors, the sustained union of two filmmakers over many years and/or films is rarer, and it warrants a closer look at the best of those recurring or long-lasting alliances. While the idea of the director usually implies one voice making the final decisions for the myriad creative components of a finished film, these directing duos prove that continuing that sense of collaboration into the chief position on a film set can bear rewarding fruit.

Here are the best directing duos of all time, ranked.

In a recent development, jean-Pierre Jeunet and Marc Caro spent years honing their singular aesthetic in short films before making their feature debut with "Delicatessen," a pitch-black comedy set in a post-apocalyptic apartment building where a butcher-landlord keeps his tenants fed by turning unsuspecting newcomers into meat. Jeunet and Caro's penchant for grotesque faces and sickly yellow lighting helped make the film a sensation, earning it four César Awards, including Best First Film and Best Original or Adapted Screenplay.

"The City of Lost Children" saw them double down on their peculiar sensibility: a fable set in a decaying port city, where a prematurely aging scientist steals children's dreams and a gentle circus strongman, played by Ron Perlman, searches for his kidnapped little brother. Its macabre, nightmarish storybook whimsy remains one of the most singular visions in French cinema — an underseen, visually stunning masterpiece.

Sources indicate that then the partnership abruptly ended. Jeunet was tapped to direct "Alien Resurrection", and his subsequent films, most famously the candy-colored "Amélie," have generally been warmer and more polished. Meanwhile, Caro's lone solo feature, the sci-fi film "Dante 01," never found the same audience. It makes for a fascinating what-if, as nobody has quite matched the blend of cruelty and tenderness the two cooked up together, and it's hard not to suspect that the grime and the heart needed each other.

John Musker and Ron Clements met at Disney while working on "The Fox and the Hound," and they went on to become one of the studio's most dependable directing teams during its biggest creative revival. They made their feature-directing debut alongside Burny Mattinson and David Michener on 1986's "The Great Mouse Detective," a Sherlock Holmes riff about a sleuthing rodent, before Clements pitched an adaptation of Hans Christian Andersen's "The Little Mermaid." Working with songwriters Howard Ashman and Alan Menken, they delivered a film that won Oscars for its score and for "Under the Sea" and helped kick off the Disney Renaissance.

Sources indicate that "Aladdin" followed in 1992. The now-iconic musical was the highest-grossing film of its year and the highest-grossing animated film to that point, earning two more Oscars for Menken's score and "A Whole New World." The duo kept working through shifting tastes, with "Hercules" in 1997 and the sci-fi swashbuckler "Treasure Planet" in 2002, which flopped but has since found its defenders. They returned to hand-drawn animation with "The Princess and the Frog" in 2009, then made their first fully computer-animated feature with "Moana," which earned an Oscar nomination for Best Animated Feature. It also spawned a widely criticized, remarkably premature live-action remake — part of a trend the pair described as "bemusing.".

Sources indicate that the pair has since retired, closing out a partnership that lasted more than three decades. Their films were defined by the fundamentals of Disney magic: musical numbers that developed the plot and emotions, and humor that never smothered the pathos underneath. Few directors have made so many movies that feel so effortlessly designed for all audiences.

Industry observers note that before they set box-office records, Joe and Anthony Russo were comedy filmmakers from Cleveland. After their micro-budget debut, "Pieces", Steven Soderbergh and George Clooney produced their second feature, "Welcome to Collinwood." The brothers broke through on television, winning an Emmy for directing the pilot of "Arrested Development," then directing the pilot of "Community" and many beloved episodes after it.

Industry observers note that that sitcom background is key to the work that followed in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, where their instincts for staging a dozen characters trading blows and punchlines helped define the quippy, ensemble-driven sensibility of their "Avengers" movies. However, that style has become a grievance among certain viewers who wish the films could escape their unrelenting sense of brand management. The brothers have cited François Truffaut and the French New Wave as major influences, but their biggest films operate within decidedly conventional blockbuster boundaries. Still, there's no denying the level of control needed to orchestrate some of the biggest hits of the 2010s.

Their post-Marvel streaming films, including "Cherry," "The Gray Man," and "The Electric State," have been considerably less successful creatively. But through their organization AGBO, they also produced the far more inventive "Everything Everywhere All at Once." With "Avengers: Doomsday" scheduled for December 2026, the brothers are once again tasked with herding Hollywood's biggest cast into something halfway coherent — a feat they've proven capable of, against all odds.

Justin Benson and Aaron Moorhead work on the principle that a tiny budget and a big idea can take you a long way. They broke out with "Resolution," which premiered at Tribeca in 2012, a lo-fi two-hander about a man who holes up in a remote cabin with his drug-addicted friend while something strange lurks beyond the walls. "Spring" followed in 2014, a Lovecraftian romance set on the Italian coast that fuses monster spectacle with the heart of a character drama. Benson typically writes and Moorhead handles cinematography, but the two co-direct and often appear on screen.

Recent findings suggest that that approach led to "The Endless," in which they play brothers returning to the cult they escaped. The film explicitly connects to "Resolution", establishing a shared cosmic-horror mythology. "Synchronic," their 2019 time-bending drug thriller with Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan, contains looser connections to that world, while the pandemic-era "Something in the Dirt" finds them starring as neighbors chasing a supernatural mystery.

Industry observers note that marvel took notice. They directed episodes of "Moon Knight" and much of the second season of "Loki," then helped rework the first season of "Daredevil: Born Again" before returning for its second. You could have worse pairs acting as custodians for one of the entertainment industry's biggest brands. Even if their Marvel work lacks the more personal flourishes of their smaller projects, you can still feel their indie-horror sensibility breaking through.

According to recent reports, daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert met at Emerson College and built their reputation on music videos, most famously DJ Snake and Lil Jon's "Turn Down for What", before making their feature debut with "Swiss Army Man," an emotionally vulnerable absurdist comedy about Paul Dano befriending a flatulent corpse played by Daniel Radcliffe. The movie's surprisingly tender treatment of shame, loneliness, and the weird stuff that makes us human earned the duo the U.S. Dramatic Directing Award at Sundance in 2016.

That set the stage for their true breakout: "Everything Everywhere All at Once" cranked their style to maximalist levels in one of the decade's most unexpected hits. Michelle Yeoh's exhausted laundromat owner is dragged across the multiverse in a hyper-stylized, daffy yet sincere family drama about an immigrant mother and her daughter facing the potential end of the world. It was A24's highest-grossing release at the time — the studio's first film to reach $100 million worldwide — and won seven of its 11 Oscar nominations, including Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Original Screenplay, plus acting wins for Yeoh, Ke Huy Quan, and Jamie Lee Curtis.

Sources indicate that that made the Daniels only the third directing pair to win Best Director, after Robert Wise & Jerome Robbins and Joel & Ethan Coen. Though prone to hyperactivity, few other filmmakers could make a hot-dog-fingers gag and a mother-daughter reconciliation feel like parts of the same carefully calculated thematic throughline. Here's hoping their next film, with Matt Damon attached, sustains that momentum.

Sources indicate that phil Lord and Christopher Miller have built a career on finding inventiveness in projects that might have become franchise mediocrity under other filmmakers. The Dartmouth classmates started in television, co-creating the short-lived MTV cult satire "Clone High," before making their feature debut with "Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs," a frantic, silly adaptation of a children's picture book filled with surprisingly clever gags and character detail.

Sources indicate that the duo kept pace: "21 Jump Street," a seemingly ill-conceived reboot of a 1980s TV drama as a buddy-cop farce, became one of the 2010s' most successful and acclaimed comedies. "The LEGO Movie," seemingly a feature-length branding exercise, became an inventive parable about creativity and conformity, launching a franchise of other LEGO films while transforming a bad premise into a cinematic miracle.

Their commitment to a distinct filmmaking voice also caused friction within the franchise machine, leading to their firing from "Solo: A Star Wars Story" late in production, though they went on to find other successes. As producers of "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse," they helped push the possibilities of mainstream animation forward. They also drew on their "Star Wars" experience in making 2026's "Project Hail Mary," a funny, meticulously crafted, heart-on-its-sleeve adaptation of Andy Weir's novel that has grossed roughly $685 million worldwide. The pair's irreverence remains central to their success: tongue-in-cheek self-awareness and a genuine love of subverting expectations have helped them turn unlikely premises into crowd-pleasers.

Lana and Lilly Wachowski came out of Chicago as comic-book obsessives, finding work as screenwriters before announcing themselves as directors with "Bound," a lean, sultry neo-noir starring Jennifer Tilly and Gina Gershon that demonstrated off their formal command on a small budget. Then came "The Matrix," the iconic 1999 sci-fi smash that fused Hong Kong martial arts, anime, and heady cyberpunk philosophy into a defining text of 2000s action cinema. Its "bullet time" effects were imitated endlessly; it broke box-office records, and cinema was never quite the same.

According to recent reports, but what really sets the sisters apart is how stubbornly they kept betting major. "Speed Racer" may have flopped on release, but it has since gained recognition as a forward-thinking work of art. Similarly, "Cloud Atlas" and "Sense8," their Netflix series about psychically linked strangers, have attracted devoted defenders of the Wachowskis' uncompromising vision. Even "Jupiter Ascending" has its champions. Their work has also invited a deeper reading of "The Matrix" as a trans allegory, something Lilly has discussed directly.

Industry observers note that the sisters have pursued separate projects in recent years. Lana directed 2021's caustically self-referential "The Matrix Resurrections" on her own, while Lilly has been developing "The Hunted," a mid-sized thriller with an all-transgender cast. Even while working apart, both continue to follow the amplified, philosophical sensibilities that made their collaborations so distinctive.

Industry observers note that widely known as engineers of feature-length anxiety attacks, Josh and Benny Safdie were among the most exciting filmmakers working in Fresh York before their broader breakthrough. They first drew attention with "Daddy Longlegs," a scrappy, semi-autobiographical portrait of a chaotic father that played Cannes' Directors' Fortnight in 2009. Then came "Heaven Knows What," a bruising drama about people struggling with heroin addiction, starring Arielle Holmes and drawn from her own experiences and writings. Their method of handheld close-ups, overlapping dialogue, and nonprofessionals cast alongside movie stars came together in "Good Time," in which Robert Pattinson plays a small-time crook losing control of one long night.

The apex was "Uncut Gems," in which Adam Sandler gave a career-defining performance as a gambling-addicted Diamond District jeweler hurtling through two hours of escalating bad decisions — a stress-riddled, darkly funny drama of street-level chaos and apprehension.

The brothers have since pursued separate directing careers, and differences in their sensibilities emerged in their solo work. Benny's "The Smashing Machine," with Dwayne Johnson as MMA fighter Mark Kerr, struggled commercially but revealed a quieter, more observant side of his filmmaking. Josh's "Marty Supreme," with Timothée Chalamet as a force of chaos, continued the streak of relentless havoc. Both films still carry the fingerprints of what the two built together: textured environments, tightly observed characters, and an acute sense of the worlds they inhabit. But the partnership that produced "Uncut Gems" remains one of the most electrifying of its era.

Industry observers note that few partnerships have been as productive or as generous to film history as Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger. Although Powell generally handled on-set direction and Pressburger originated many of their stories, they famously shared writing, producing, and directing credit during their peak years as the Archers. Powell, an Englishman who learned his craft on British quota quickies, and Pressburger, a Hungarian screenwriter who fled Nazi Germany, first teamed up in 1939. Pressburger later won an Oscar for the original story of 1941's "49th Parallel," and in the early 1940s they formed their production company, the Archers, whose films opened with an arrow striking a target.

It has been revealed that that led to one of the great runs in British cinema: the wartime satire "The Life and Death of Colonel Blimp," the pastoral "A Canterbury Tale," the romance "I Know Where I'm Going!," and "A Matter of Life and Death," a fantasy about a pilot who cheats death. "Black Narcissus" won Oscars for Jack Cardiff's cinematography and Alfred Junge's art direction, while "The Red Shoes" remains an utterly dazzling film about artistic obsession, with its nearly 17-minute ballet sequence nestled inside a classical yet fantastical melodrama.

Their main partnership ended after 1957's "Ill Met by Moonlight," though they collaborated again on smaller projects, including "They're a Weird Mob" and "The Boy Who Turned Yellow." Powell's solo thriller "Peeping Tom" was so reviled by British critics that it badly damaged his career, though it has since been rediscovered as a masterpiece, thanks in no small part to Martin Scorsese.

It has been revealed that joel and Ethan Coen have long worked like one filmmaker with two heads, though Directors Guild rules obscured that for two decades by crediting Joel as director and Ethan as producer. The two also shared editing duties under the pseudonym Roderick Jaynes, a nonexistent editor who nonetheless earned Oscar nominations for "Fargo" and "No Country for Old Men." They finally received joint directing credit with 2004's "The Ladykillers." By then, the work had long spoken for itself: "Blood Simple" and "Raising Arizona" announced a pair of formalists with a wicked sense of humor, and "Barton Fink" swept Cannes in 1991.

Working frequently with cinematographer Roger Deakins, they moved between screwball comedy ("Raising Arizona," "Burn After Reading"), gangster pictures ("Miller's Crossing"), and Westerns ("True Grit") with unmatched formal and tonal precision. Few filmmakers could make movies as equally iconic as "The Big Lebowski" and "No Country for Old Men," works at opposite ends of the tonal spectrum that still feel unmistakably of a piece with the brothers' sardonic, philosophical sensibility.

After 2018's "The Ballad of Buster Scruggs," the brothers pursued solo directing projects, with Joel making "The Tragedy of Macbeth" and Ethan making "Drive-Away Dolls" and "Honey Don't!" But in October 2026, while receiving the Lumière Prize in Lyon, they said they planned to direct another film together. Joel's upcoming "Jack of Spades," which Ethan co-wrote and Netflix intends to release theatrically in fall 2027, is still a solo directing project, but their reunion comments suggest another collaboration may be ahead. Hopefully they'll add another movie to a remarkable joint filmography, which we've ranked in full.

In a recent development, the final weeks of Dancing with the Stars always feature really tough eliminations. However, the last few on the 2026 TV schedule have been brutal. During a conversation with TV Insider, Ribeiro shared his thoughts on this, and the conversation he had with the pro and Glee actor after they found out they’d be going home. He stated:.

Sources indicate that there was a lot of sharing of disappointment in my heart, what they did right, and just letting them know that I care and that I’m saddened for them. Or with them. I’ll leave it at that.

In a recent development, I’m also saddened for them. While Harry and Jenna always had some of the best routines of every episode, their DWTS journey was plagued by some controversy and intense online discourse.
