📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Warning! This post contains SPOILERS for Midnight Spider-Man #2.

Marvel's newly introduced Midnight Universe has begun, featuring dark and horrific new takes on classic heroes in an alt universe unlike anything we've seen before. However, the latest problem of Midnight Spider-Man has confirmed that villains are receiving just as terrifying redesigns as well.

Industry observers note that as seen in the first issue of Midnight Spider-Man, this dark new continuity's Peter Parker has become a truly grotesque David Cronenberg-style body-horror version of a human-spider hybrid, the result of twisted Oscorp experiments in the pursuit of eternal life. Contrasting with the classic Spider-Man motto, "With great power comes great responsibility", the darker world and circumstances surrounding Peter have instead instilled the phrase: "power makes monsters." Now that Peter has become a monster himself, his future looks to be all kinds of horrifying.

Now, Midnight Spider-Man #2 by Phillip Kennedy Johnson and Scietronc has debuted a brand-fresh version of Doctor Octopus, one that's easily more disturbing than any version seen before in the pages of Marvel Comics.

Industry observers note that the story in Midnight Spider-Man #2 is aptly titled "The Eight-Handed Man," giving readers our first look at Otto Octavius and his role as a lead researcher at Oscorp behind the Augustine Project and the manufacturer's mission to achieve eternal life via twisted experiments involving animal-human hybrids. Initially shown as a reclusive germaphobe who hates interacting with foreign contaminants and individuals outside his lab, an incredibly diminutive Otto keeps himself isolated behind glass with various metal pins sticking out of his head.

Sources indicate that the lab itself is full of dissection tables with various genetically mutated specimens that have gruesomely been ripped apart by his "assistants". Rather than having his traditional four robotic arms, this dark newly introduced version of Doctor Octopus controls four human beings through cybernetic brain implants somewhat resembling the classic tentacles. All of their individual humanity looks to have been stripped away, leaving them as nothing more than remote-controlled extensions of Octavius. Likewise, Octavius even threatens to turn Felicia Hardy into his next assistant should she fail to recover the spider that escaped in the new series' first problem.

Having wound up in Peter's backpack, the large radioactive spider ultimately fused with Peter and embedded itself in his chest. Right now unaware of this monstrous transformation, Otto desperately wants the spider back, and for Felicia to ensure that Peter signs a contract of employment to start working at Oscorp itself.

Ultimately, this super dark intro for Midnight Doc Ock makes it clear that as monstrous as Peter Parker might have just become in this dark new universe, Oscorp is the true and much bigger monster behind it all.

Nevertheless, it's extremely unsettling to see "Spider-Man" launching himself at Felicia Hardy (perhaps a future Midnight Black Cat?) and her men when they come to Peter's house, ripping the security guards to shreds with all kinds of blood and gore, leaving the house with only Felicia alive and paralyzed with fear. Clearly, this is going to be one of the scariest and most violent Spider-Man ever seen.

With the first problem strongly implying that the spider killed Uncle Ben before fusing with Peter, the grief and horror that will come once Peter discovers this will likely be what fully turns him against Oscorp (he had been more optimistic about joining them and turning them into a force for good from within, despite Uncle Ben suing them for their involvement in the deaths of Peter's parents).

Assuming Peter will find a way to control or at least direct his monstrous impulses toward those responsible, it follows that Midnight Spider-Man will likely wage a one-man war against Oscorp in future complications. As such, his newly introduced status as a human-spider hybrid will no doubt be seen as a major breakthrough by Octavius, making a confrontation between the two more than inevitable in the issues to come.

Midnight Spider-Man #2 is on sale now from Marvel Comics.

Tech Report: The Method-Dressing Madness Behind Mckenna Grace‘s 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Press Tour Looks

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping press tour began, Mckenna Grace knew she wanted to be method dressed for her appearances.
  • With the upcoming Hunger Games film, it’s Grace’s turn to adopt the trend.
  • In a wide-ranging conversation, Dickson breaks down all the looks that set the Hunger Games fans’ hearts aflame, from Rue’s blue dress to Katniss’ Mockingjay gown, and all the threads that came together for Grace’s most memorable press appearances yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping press tour began, Mckenna Grace knew she wanted to be method dressed for her appearances. Made a household term by Law Roach and Zendaya, method dressing is when actors wear looks that pay homage to the film or show they’re promoting: See Zendaya’s on-theme looks across red carpets for Dune, Spiderman, and The Odyssey for a slew of examples.

With the upcoming Hunger Games film, it’s Grace’s turn to adopt the trend. A super fan of the Suzanne Collins book series and their film adaptations, Grace—who plays District 12 tribute Maysilee Donner—took a hand in the styling for her press run, weaving easter eggs into every look. Her stylist, Molly Dickson, was up for the challenge of translating Grace’s deep-cut references into custom and archival looks from Monique Lhuillier, Gucci, Celine and more.

In a wide-ranging conversation, Dickson breaks down all the looks that set the Hunger Games fans’ hearts aflame, from Rue’s blue dress to Katniss’ Mockingjay gown, and all the threads that came together for Grace’s most memorable press appearances yet.

Vanity Fair: How did you get into styling?

Molly Dickson: I went to college in Minnesota and my major was advertising. Two weeks before I graduated, I called my mom and said, "I'm not into this. I don't wanna do advertising." She said, "Well, what do you wanna do?" I told her, "I wanna do fashion. I wanna go to Latest York." She said, "No, absolutely not.".

Right after I graduated, I went to LA, this was 2009 during the recession, and no one was hiring. I got an internship at Marie Claire in New York, and enrolled back into college to get school credit to intern at Hearst. I worked at Marie Claire as a market assistant for almost two years, and then I left and assisted Leslie Fremar for seven years. That's when I fell in love with celebrity. Then ten years ago, I went off on my own.

What would you say are your aesthetic influences as a stylist?

Sources indicate that my personal style relates very similarly to Sadie Sink's style, very effortless. She always wants to be very comfortable and easy, never anything frilly or over the top. Just a simple, beautiful dress, and you let it speak for itself.

According to recent reports, mckenna is a big fan of the original film series, so it’s clear you’re pulling from there as influences when dressing her. Is it a collaborative process when coming to one of these referential looks?

She's obviously a very huge fan of the franchise. We actually started having conversations about this tour in April, which is very early to start having conversations. I could just sense her excitement around it. She started sending me mood boards, and I actually looked back today at the mood board and it was, it was a lot of Katniss Everdeen. It had Joanna on it, and it was filled with these really strong female characters from the franchise.

What she really wanted to hit was Katniss’ wedding gown look and the Mockingjay look with the wings. I was really stumped on how to pull that off without making it overly costumey.

According to recent reports, mckenna kept asking, "What's going on with those?" I knew the vision, but I didn't know how to execute it. I was working with Keke Palmer and the designer Michael Ngo. He was making some cool music costumes for Keke, and I asked, "Michael, could you make this silver piece?" 'Cause I really had no idea how to get it done.

In a recent development, he said, “I don't think I can do that. You know what? Just give me a day, let me play around with it." That night, he said, "I figured it out." We got the piece and I thought, "Okay, it needs to be a wedding dress under,” so I reached out to all the bridal houses. I wanted it to be vintage because it would tell a pretty story. Monique [Lhuillier] ended up sending a ton of wedding gowns, and the day before Mckenna came in for the fitting, I actually tried the wedding dresses on myself with the silver piece.

Industry observers note that I sent Mckenna five dresses, and the one that she ended up wearing, she mentioned, "That's it. I don't even need to try anything else. That's the one I'm gonna wear." Then, it was a matter of finding the right event to wear it to because it’s pretty nice, very dramatic.

It has been revealed that she was in Paris for the Miu Miu show, and I brought it there because she had the Hunger Games Museum event. It was a whole conversation with her team, like, "Is it the right moment? Is it too much for this event?" Her PR said, "No, this is the perfect moment. It's the best way to kick off the tour." The response with the Hunger Games fans—I have never seen anything like it before, ever.

What was the experience of having her be such a big part of the styling process?

It makes my job so fun because she is so passionate about it and she loves Hunger Games so much, even just finding subtle nods back to the movie. She would say, "I wanna do a ladybug look." Thom Browne did that amazing ladybug dress, I thought, "That's so cool, but it's not really her personal aesthetic." So it’s finding ways to keep it still true to her personal style while maintaining the nods to the film.

It has been revealed that the way you seem to understand Mckenna feels something similar to the connection between Katniss and Cinna in The Hunger Games. When pulling looks for her, what comes into play? How do you make her come through and not be lost in the lore of the stories or the dress?

It has been revealed that mckenna had said that she maybe wanted to do a red or a dark pink feather look because in the books [Maysilee] gets attacked by the red birds which are like flamingos. I'm pulling in all these red feather dresses and on the runway, this one dress looked amazing. Mckenna said, “That's perfect for the flamingo reference.”.

It has been revealed that but we put it on her and it was so substantial, and she's so petite so she was just getting swarmed. I stated, “Let"s not force it.” The goal was for her to feel comfortable in the look rather than just getting each reference.

The public has been really excited about these looks. Are you thinking about the response to the looks when you’re putting them together?

There's been some conversations in a fitting, like, "Oh, the Hunger Games fans are gonna get this." They're gonna see the inspiration, they're gonna understand it.

But I wouldn't say we're choosing a look because ‘Oh, this is gonna go viral to the Hunger Games community.’ Mckenna is a super fan herself so if she's getting excited about the look, everyone else that's a fan of the franchise is gonna get excited about the look.

Mckenna Grace in Betsey Johnson.

Do you feel any pressure to top the last outfit after each premiere?

Yes. I think it was Paris because that wedding dress did get so much press. In that fitting, it felt like, "We gotta keep our game up high." It's been really fun for my team and market assistants because a lot of the girls that work with me are huge fans of the movie. They're not even seeing it as work. They're like, "Oh my God, this is so exciting. Look at this. This looks like this from the movie.".

Recent findings suggest that what was the inspiration to do method dressing for this press run? What do you think is the value?

Mckenna knew back in April, she noted, "I wanna do method for this." I personally did not read the books. I'm a visual person, so I've seen all the movies. Lionsgate was able to let me go with the cast when they first saw the movie because my agent was like, "Molly needs to go to the movie to get inspired before this press tour. She can't do a method dressing press tour without seeing the movie.".

Even as the tour was going on, Mckenna kept sending me newly introduced references and quotes from the book and stuff like that.

Recent findings suggest that what made you take it to the next level? From paying homage to not only characters, but the actual actors from the films like Jennifer Lawrence at the 2011 Oscars to even dressing like set pieces from the film.

That was all Mckenna's vision. On her first mood board, she had a lot of Jennifer Lawrence's red carpet moments because she's such a huge fan of Katniss and Jennifer Lawrence.

With the Rue reference, Mckenna thought that color was just very Hunger Games. It wasn't until she put the dress on, her mom said, "Wait, this is Rue's dress." So that was just fate. I would love to take credit for that.

Why do you think that this styling has generated so much attention?

Recent findings suggest that I think it’s when you do method dressing for such a massive franchise and you really are passionate about it. The thing is that Mckenna is so excited and passionate about this movie. She has said, “I didn't think that I would love doing fittings so much. I used to hate doing fittings.”.

Mckenna Grace in Elisabetta Franchi.

According to recent reports, because every look is so intentionally tied back to Hunger Games and she's such a big fan, it's literally like playing dress up with her. I think the fans see it, she's so relatable because she's a fan that all these fans think, "Wow, like, she's a fan and she got to do this." She’s the fangirl living out her dream, and the fans are excited for her that she finally gets to do this.

What do you think are the best kinds of projects to implement method dressing with/works best with? What does it work best with?

Sources indicate that I think the big movies that already have a fan base, like Barbie or Wednesday, Being able to pull inspiration from existing books or films makes it so much easier for a stylist rather than a movie that no one's seen before. There's no curiosity or momentum about it because you're starting from scratch, whereas Hunger Games, Barbie, Wednesday, there's already a level of expectation.

Industry observers note that the looks for this press run have been a mix of archival, new, and custom pieces. How do you make that choice? How important is it for you to create an archive for Mckenna?

According to recent reports, it kind of is a mix of what we’re able to source. McKenna really wanted to pay homage to Joanna's character with that scene where she's like, "My stylist is always putting me in trees." She's like, "I wanna do a tree reference." And I'm like, "How in the world am I gonna find a fashion reference that's a tree that's not a costume?".

I love the challenge of sourcing the market, and so do the girls on my team. I think it was 2011 Phoebe Philo where Celine did some tree references in the collection. But just because we find it online doesn't mean that we can get it. So then it's reaching out to every vintage dealer, every rental house, asking, "Do you guys have anything like this?" And they might have it, but they're like, "It's already gone, someone has it." I ended up actually finding the Celine tree dress on the RealReal, and I bought it. I love RealReal.

It has been revealed that what is your approach to dressing different clients? For instance, you mentioned Sadie Sink earlier, can you walk me through how that process differs from Mckenna?

It's very different between each girl. I let them set the pace. If they wanna be involved, great. If they just wanna show up to the fitting and not even know what's gonna be there, I try to accommodate whatever direction they wanna go. I have one client that literally last week has sent me over 200 references of dresses that she wants, and another girl that's like, “I really don't care. Whatever you tell me to wear, I'll wear it.”.

Recent findings suggest that every girl is different, and what makes my job so interesting is that it's not the same. Everyone has very different styles. I think the most vital part of a job as a stylist is to keep their style true to them and not just force my style onto them. McKenna's way more girly, Sadie is a little bit more casual, it’s just taking their style and elevating it a little bit.

Industry observers note that will you do any looks inspired by Mckenna’s character Maysilee? The looks have been mostly referential to things and people from past stories. Are there influences of Maysilee in the looks that fans haven't been able to pick up on because the film wasn’t out yet?

Sources indicate that in a couple days, she’ll be in Miami for press, and she's wearing a very Maysilee inspired, purple Miu Miu dress that has a white collar. When she wears it, everyone's gonna be like, "Oh, that's Maysilee." She really wanted to have flowers and necklaces because Maysilee is really into jewelry, so it’s very light and flowery.

Can you break down the outfit for the New York City premiere?

We are doing the Mockingjay dress, the one with the wings, and that was another thing that I was very stumped on. I'm like, "What designer's gonna make these wings?" I had this woman in LA who does wings, she's done Halloween costumes and music videos.

Mckenna Grace in Pamella Roland.

According to recent reports, in the first fitting, I pulled this navy Pamella Roland gown. The fabric is really, really cool. It's like a shimmery kind of organza. I thought, "That's the right color,” but I wanted it to be strapless. I went back to Pamella Roland and they were like, "We can make it in strapless." Mckenna was very keen on having some sort of embellishment to replicate Katniss because she had screen printing on the gown and it kind of looks like wings in a way.

Industry observers note that pamela then drew all these CADs with diamond wings on it, and then we got the wings made. We did the final fitting and I almost started to cry. Her mom's taking videos and it's epic. It's so exciting because the fans were doing polls on what she's gonna wear to the premiere.

It's full circle, we started with the wedding dress, Mckenna did the fire gown, and then we ended with the Mockingjay dress.

What was the hardest look to pull together?

Mckenna Grace in custom Cong Tri.

I think design-wise, it was the fire gown.

Sources indicate that getting the fire printed on the fabric was really hard. I had a while back done a custom Cong Tri gown for Cami Mendes for the Masters of the Universe tour. It was like a gold beaded gown, and I remember I really liked the fabrics that they used for it.

So when I was thinking of who could do this fire gown, I reached out to them first, and I'm like, "Can you guys do something that looks like a fire? Like, she's literally on fire." And they're like, "No. We don't think we can." And again, they were like, "Give us some time." They came back and said, "We did all these testing on the fabric." I'm like, "Yeah, you did it. You did it.".

In a recent development, what's really funny is we were at a fitting at Mckenna's house with the fire gown in a garment bag, and one of her friends stopped by. It was just a tip of the dress showing and her friend said, "Oh my God, you got a fire gown." Then I thought, "Okay, people are gonna get it.".

#51347. 8 Must-Play JRPGs for People With Real-Life Schedules

8 Must-Play JRPGs for People With Real-Life Schedules

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it’s 9:15 on a Wednesday night.
  • But there are some games in the genre you can bend to fit your week.
  • How do you finish an RPG that can run past 100 hours when you have only 30 spare minutes — on a good night?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s 9:15 on a Wednesday night. The dishes are done. You have about 45 minutes before bed, and you’re a JRPG fan (or you were, when you had more time). JRPGs tend to demand dozens of hours from players — and they can make it very difficult to pause, as some of them will interrupt you with a battle every few steps.

But there are some games in the genre you can bend to fit your week. These eight JRPGs split their stories into chapters, let you switch off random battles, speed up fights, or save almost anywhere. Even if you press start at 9:20, you can still be in bed by 10.

How do you finish an RPG that can run past 100 hours when you have only 30 spare minutes — on a good night? Dragon Quest 11: Echoes of an Elusive Age can do it, as long as you play it in small pieces. You’re the Luminary, a silent hero raised in the village of Cobblestone who learns he's the reincarnation of a legendary hero destined to fight the Dark One. Your trip across the bright, friendly land of Erdrea builds a party one self-contained chapter at a time, each with its own local problems to solve. To make this significant game work in small doses, pick either 3D mode or 2D mode and stay there. (Progress carries over poorly when you switch.) You can also raise the battle speed, which can make fights up to three times faster and cuts down on grinding. Then save at a Sacred Stone, and treat each stop as a chapter break.

Recent findings suggest that this game opens with a disaster: the Great Chasm swallows a village, and a shepherd named Tiz is the only survivor. You play as Tiz, who teams up with Agnes, a vestal of the Wind Crystal, to free four elemental crystals that darkness has swallowed. Edea, a defector from the Eternian Sky Knights, and Ringabel, an amnesiac who carries a journal that seems to record future events, join the party along the way.

Sources indicate that this remaster explicitly hands you the controls for your schedule. You can set the encounter rate from 50 to 200 percent at any time on the field map, push battle speed to 4x, and let auto-battle repeat your last actions. Turn the dial to match whatever time and energy you happen to have when you’re ready to play.

Time to beat: Between 15-30 hours per game.

It has been revealed that random battles are the reason many people bounce off old JRPGs. The Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster series gives you a switch for those random encounters, so — problem solved. The series remasters Final Fantasy 1 through 6 in 2D pixel art. Start with the first game, where four heroes of light must save the world by recovering four elemental crystals from castles, towers, and mountains. As you wend your way through the game’s dungeons, pull up the Boost menu. With it, you can turn random encounters on or off at any time and raise EXP, gil, and ability point gains up to four times. When your four heroes need levels before the next crystal, raise the EXP boost and turn encounters back on. Switch encounters off, walk to the next town, and get your evening back.

Industry observers note that art aficionados-slash-JRPG-fans rejoice: This game’s distinctive 160-plus locations are handmade dioramas that were photographed and converted into 3D worlds. Here, you play Leo, an amnesiac who sets out to recover his memories while a mechanical infection called Mechteria spreads across the land. Hironobu Sakaguchi produced it and wrote the story. He also included a scheduling trick: the Dimengeon Machine. This machine stores the enemies you’ve already fought, so you can reach chests and save points without stopping for random encounters. It also fills swiftly late in the game, so empty it at the start of a long session and leave it on while you walk. Here’s your basic strategy: Walk first, fight later.

It has been revealed that A magical explosion ends a war between three kingdoms while killing thousands. A mercenary named Glenn sets out to find and destroy the crystal weapon behind the detonation. He’s joined by a princess who left her castle to see the world and a master thief . There are fights with mechs in their future. Lots of them.

It has been revealed that chained Echoes is a 16-bit-style JRPG set on the continent of Valandis. While your characters are committed to fighting, you don’t have to be: This game allows you to skip random encounters, long treks to inns, and endless grinds. Enemies stay visible on the map, and your party recovers health between fights. You can save anywhere, and fast travel is free once the introductory sequence ends. Combat is turn-based and fast, and an Overdrive gauge keeps you thinking about which skills you use. Fight, save, and close the lid. Come back tomorrow (or whenever). Repeat.

According to recent reports, crono goes to the Millennial Fair and ends up four centuries in the past. (We’ve all been there.) During a friend’s scientific demonstration, a girl named Marle is pulled through a time rift, and Crono follows. His chase to save Marle becomes a quest to save the planet’s future, with stops in prehistory, the Middle Ages, the distant future, and the End of Time. Chrono Trigger is one of the shortest games here, at about 16-32 hours for the main story. The Steam version saves your progress both at dedicated save points and when you quit. It also saves automatically as you move around the map. Know that time does keep moving while you’re in a fight, so make sure to hit pause whenever life interrupts. As it turns out, saving the future is easier when you can pause the present, anyway.

Industry observers note that on the continent of Orsterra, Ophilia the cleric takes her church's pilgrimage, Cyrus the scholar hunts for a vanished tome, and Tressa the merchant follows the author of an anonymous diary. Olberic, a former knight, takes up his sword again when bandits kidnap a boy. Primrose the dancer plots revenge, Alfyn the apothecary wants to ease suffering, Therion the thief needs three Dragonstones to win his freedom, and H'aanit the hunter searches for her missing master.

Each of the eight heroes’ stories has four chapters. Nearly every chapter follows the same loop: Enter a town, talk to people, clear a dungeon, beat a boss. That makes each boss fight your stopping point. Recommended-level gates mean you'll rotate between heroes, so no single story stalls. Save at the white feather icons near dungeons and towns. Play through one chapter whenever you have a free-ish night, and Orsterra will be yours before you know it.

According to recent reports, can’t commit to one long story? Try seven short ones. Live A Live sends seven heroes through seven eras: a martial artist entering a global fighting tournament in the present day, a conflicted agent in the twilight of Edo Japan, a wanderer with a bounty on his head in the Wild West, a psychic in the near future, a spaceship crew whose AI turns lethal, a martial arts master in Imperial China searching for a disciple, and cavemen in prehistory. Each of the seven core chapters stands alone, so you can play them in any order. The gameplay in each chapter varies a bit: One is a straight run of fights that takes about a half hour. Others are mini RPGs with random encounters and some grinding, so perhaps it’s best to save those for a weekend.

#51346. The Downfall Of The Terminator Franchise Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (887 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashfilm ↗ Open Full Page

The Downfall Of The Terminator Franchise Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it's a question which has plagued the "Terminator" franchise for decades: why hasn't anyone been able to top the first two films?
  • The ultimate problem with the "Terminator" franchise is twofold.
  • In a recent development, it's true that the general tone of the first two "Terminator" films is a dark, brooding, horrific one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it's a question which has plagued the "Terminator" franchise for decades: why hasn't anyone been able to top the first two films? Setting aside the usual caveat that no sequel can hope to match the dizzying heights of some of the most influential sci-fi/action/horror movies of all time, it's a decent question. After all, every "Terminator" movie save one has involved star Arnold Schwarzenegger in a key role, so it's not like his absence has hurt the series. And even though the return of another key actor in the series, Linda Hamilton, helped 2019's "Terminator: Dark Fate," that film still had its complications. A conventional wisdom answer to the problem of rescuing the "Terminator" series is that the original creator/director James Cameron should fully come back and make another installment, yet his involvement with "Dark Fate" means success wouldn't necessarily be guaranteed.

The ultimate problem with the "Terminator" franchise is twofold. One matter is the staggering example set by the first two films, which would be hard for any franchise to overcome. The other concerns the one moment that the downfall of the franchise can be traced back to, which is ironically one of the moments most cited by fans as a highlight of the series: the ending of 2003's "Terminator 3: Rise of the Machines." To be fair, most of "Terminator 3," despite its decent quality, is to blame for putting the franchise on a path it can't quite escape from. Yet it's the ending, as bold as it is, which struck a deterministic note that ended up being too harsh for the series to bear. "Terminator" has always been dark, yet its hopeful subtext is key to its recipe, and that's something which has been left out of every installment since "Terminator 2.".

In a recent development, it's true that the general tone of the first two "Terminator" films is a dark, brooding, horrific one. After all, these are movies in which Linda Hamilton's Sarah Connor is on the run for her life from an unstoppable killing machine, where either she or her young son John suddenly find themselves having to survive the threats of a dark future while having little help from the modern day around them. Yet an important thing to remember about "The Terminator" is that Skynet's strategy to assassinate Sarah by sending a Terminator back in time was only implemented because John wins the war against the machines in the future. "The Terminator" is a time travel story, and is thus subject to the various paradoxes inherent to the genre. Yet its tale has a deterministic logic to it, one which is predicated on humans surviving despite their near-annihilation by the machines.

"Terminator 3" effectively undoes the ambiguous hopeful ending of "Terminator 2," where Sarah and John had possibly prevented Judgment Day for good. While the third film's logic is sound from a time travel point of view (i.e. how could any "Terminator" movie have happened if Judgement Day never does), it does make "Terminator 2" feel too much like it was all for nought. Adding to that quiet despair is the bigger tragedy of actually seeing Judgment Day occur, meaning that the efforts of a now adult John (Nick Stahl) to try and stop it from happening again make not just "Terminator 2" but most of "Terminator 3" feel deflating. The ending of "Terminator 3" is a great example of how a cool twist can work logically, yet emotionally undermine a film (and, in this case, a franchise) too much.

The first two "Terminator" films leaned into the time travel paradox by presenting a deterministic situation while supporting free will. "There's no fate but what we make for ourselves" is a key phrase which can be interpreted several ways, as either a bitter observation or a message of hope. While the deterministic path that "Terminator 3" and "Terminator Salvation" took was logically sound, they didn't provide enough of the aspirational side; the latter film was a time travel story in subtext only.

Industry observers note that the next two movies in the franchise course-corrected in a bizarre way, embracing the wide-open possibilities of the series' time travel component with little to no regard for the characters or the audience. "Genisys" is too pleased with its twists to let any of them land emotionally. In comparison, "Dark Fate" has much richer characterizations, yet it alienates from the opening twist, and turns the series' lore on its head in a way that doesn't fully land. The franchise's one shining moment post-"Terminator 2," the TV series "Terminator: The Sarah Connor Chronicles," was sadly canceled just as the intricate narrative it weaved was bearing the type of lore-changing fruit that "Genisys" and "Dark Fate" tried too hard to grow.

According to recent reports, in general, the "Terminator" sequels after "Judgment Day" have attempted to serve both the series' deterministic and free will concepts, which are inherently paradoxical. So, while every one of the "Terminator" sequels have introduced some fascinating (and occasionally excellent) ideas, they all revolve around an inescapable fate, whether it's one that already happened or one that will happen. While I believe the series' fate could still be changed, it's ironic that the thing we're hoping gets saved is now the "Terminator" films themselves.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that two things can be true at once with Tom Hardy: he vanishes into roles with all the finesse of a deep-cover spy, and we never forget who we're watching. Such awareness isn't a negative, though; when Hardy signs his name to a project, said story arrives at our doorsteps with the rubber-stamped guarantee that he has wholeheartedly thrown himself into the character. The palpably realistic and sometimes avant-garde mannerisms, voice shifts, and physical transformations seem effortless, but audiences know the road to Hardy's results is all dedicated effort.

In 2009, right before Hardy vaulted into household name status, he left his mark on one of classic literature's most infamous, analyzed, and misrepresented figures. Emily Brontë simultaneously refined and created an archetype with Wuthering Heights, and countless riffs on Heathcliff — equal parts brooding antagonist and tragic antihero — have followed in her landmark footsteps since 1847. Every time a new movie or television adaptation rolls around, actors covet the ingeniously rich part. Many have delivered fine performances, but only a handful have gotten close enough to graze their fingertips against Wuthering Heights' stormy and tormented soul.

And while Brontë's descriptions of Heathcliff contain a degree of racial ambiguity, she inarguably establishes him as a man of color — an imperative fact that the majority of filmmakers have neglected. Without ever diminishing or excusing such consistent whitewashing, Hardy's take on Healthcliff is also one of the most definitive interpretations by far. The two-part miniseries itself remains the adaptational gold standard to date, too — desolate, macabre, bitter, thematically accurate, and feverishly intoxicating.

Wuthering Heights is a magnificently tricky puzzle to crack on the page and even more difficult to translate onto the screen. Rather than the straightforward doomed love story it has often been mistaken for, Brontë's morbid and profoundly thoughtful work uncompromisingly interrogates class hierarchy, generational trauma, domestic and systemic abuse cycles, gender and race, obsessive grief, all-consuming revenge, and psychosexual subtext.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

Recent findings suggest that you want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

According to recent reports, you do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

Recent findings suggest that the 2009 limited series does justice to her vast scope, truncates little, and softens nothing. Writer Peter Bowker achieves maximum faithfulness, preserving the thematic integrity in general and by including the crucial plot beats other adaptations abandon for the sake of streamlined simplicity; eliminating the second generation of children negates Brontë's prevailing points. Bowker's scripts employ a flashback structure instead of a traditional chronological approach, which prevents the second episode from losing momentum and gives both halves equal weight.

Coky Giedroyc's direction might not contain the same level of moody lavishness as a high-budget Hollywood affair, but for 2009-era network television, the atmosphere is precisely on point. By day, the visuals luxuriate in the windswept and rocky Yorkshire Moors like the terrain is a private paradise; by night, those same locations drip with an ominous, rain-soaked, Gothic chill no warm coat or feeble lantern light can protect against. If anything, the production's subtle efficiency enables the performers to sell the emotional turbulence with maximum artistic freedom and commitment.

According to recent reports, in a way, Heathcliff is a perfect example of Hardy both playing against type and tapping into his exact strengths. It's a demanding role, and he unearths the complete spectrum — every paradoxical layer of aching loneliness, tender desperation, wounded pride, extreme intelligence, seething spite, and punitive cruelty. A defiant survivor of abuse, ostracization, and rejection, he's understated and internalized at one moment, his eyes hollowed out by the phantoms of regret, before gliding straight into visceral rage. He can invade and dominate a room through the sheer force of his insidious physicality, yet still exert a seductively appealing gravitational pull.

And a Heathcliff, of course, is nothing without his beloved Cathy Earnshaw (Charlotte Riley). Another exceedingly intricate and tricky role, Riley makes Cathy as irresistible, isolated, selfish, jealous, and demanding as she should be. The woman's whims are as untethered as the wind and as dangerous as a sparking live wire; she relishes exerting control by playfully toying with her lovers. In tandem, Riley sells the overwhelming sincerity of Cathy's volatile emotions; it's readily apparent and tragic why her gilded-cage aristocratic life kills her unsatiated spirit long before it kills her body. The war between her contradictory desires — liberated freedom versus conforming to society's standards for financial security and comfort — plays across her face like an Expressionist painting.

In a recent development, hardy and Riley's chemistry is so naturally thunderous that the pair married five years after filming Wuthering Heights. They capture the characters' star-crossed toxicity in all its smothering closeness, from two young and powerless outcasts who forge a home together and consume each other's chaotic passion like oxygen, to venomous snakes inflicting reciprocal misery until both parties self-destruct. Cathy and Heathcliff is no great love story by any aspirational or enviable measure. However, as terrible, damaged, and lost people who recognize their twin flame, but ruin the solace for which they yearn, they're perfect for each other — as near-perfect as this masterpiece adaptation.

#51344. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1291 w)

Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font.
  • It has been revealed that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • Industry observers note that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

It has been revealed that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

Industry observers note that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

In a recent development, those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

In a recent development, while most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

Industry observers note that this pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

In a recent development, if there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

According to recent reports, one of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

Industry observers note that in every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

In a recent development, to a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What a difference seven-odd months make.
  • You see, one of the joys of live theater is bearing witness to a performer who's captured the music of an uncommonly gifted playwright's dialogue.
  • Recent findings suggest that lonergan remembered this and cast Ruffalo in his 2000 film classic "You Can Count on Me." Then, when the actor started booking studio gigs, Lonergan cooked up "Margaret." It's a Fresh York City epic about a teenager (Anna Paquin) who struggles to cope with a fatal city bus accident she inadvertently put in motion, with Ruffalo playing the bus driver whose ill-advised, but innocuous, flirtation leads to a horrible accident on the Upper West Side of Manhattan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What a difference seven-odd months make. Near the tail-end of September 2011, Fox Searchlight dumped Kenneth Lonergan's "Margaret" six years after it was filmed, only for its star, Mark Ruffalo, to Hulk-out in "The Avengers" the following May. But even so, Lonergan's movie — one of the best of the 21st Century — deserves so much better than to merely be remembered as a box office bomb.

You see, one of the joys of live theater is bearing witness to a performer who's captured the music of an uncommonly gifted playwright's dialogue. In my lifetime, I've seen Philip Seymour Hoffman and John C. Reilly make a meal out of Sam Shepard's "True West," Rosemary Harris and Elaine Stritch tear up Edward Albee's "A Delicate Balance," and Jeffrey Wright and Don Cheadle set the stage ablaze with Suzan-Lori Parks' "Topdog/Underdog." On that same level, a late-20-something Ruffalo caused an off-Broadway stir in the fall of 1996 with his portrayal of troubled teenager Walter Straub in Lonergan's finely wrought drama "This Is Our Youth." He exuded shaggily handsome charm as a purposeless kid with a short-term game blueprint that involves absconding with $15,000 of his wealthy dirtbag father's money.

Recent findings suggest that lonergan remembered this and cast Ruffalo in his 2000 film classic "You Can Count on Me." Then, when the actor started booking studio gigs, Lonergan cooked up "Margaret." It's a Fresh York City epic about a teenager (Anna Paquin) who struggles to cope with a fatal city bus accident she inadvertently put in motion, with Ruffalo playing the bus driver whose ill-advised, but innocuous, flirtation leads to a horrible accident on the Upper West Side of Manhattan. This is as close to a clean logline as you can get with Lonergan's rich, sophisticated text, which baffled its dilettante, bigoted, multi-millionaire producer Gary Gilbert.

"Margaret" was a talent magnet. Kenneth Lonergan's blisteringly brilliant screenplay drew in Mark Ruffalo, Paquin, Matt Damon, J. Smith Cameron, Allison Janney, Matthew Broderick, Jean Reno, and Rosemarie DeWitt. The great Jeannie Berlin, a Best Supporting Actress Oscar nominee for her knockout work in 1972's "The Heartbreak Kid," also appeared in the movie (her first since 1990's "In the Spirit"), and she was dubbed Best Supporting Actress by the Village Voice Film Poll for her turn as the sister of the victim killed in the aforementioned accident.

"Margaret" is a drama without villains. Anna Paquin's Lisa is a misguided and impulsive teenager. She is in search of justice where nothing of the sort can be found and tracks down Ruffalo's bus driver. He's well aware of the threat she poses to his steady bus-driving job, though, and shoos her away. But she persists, and her version of the events of that deadly day aren't entirely wrong, yet she still shares some responsibility. Yet, she can't accept that, so her catharsis will not arrive via a conviction.

Structurally, "Margaret" splits its time between Lisa's errant pursuit of justice and her mother (Cameron) as she tries to connect with a suave suitor played by Reno. Everyone loses. But this loss forges a stronger bond between mother and daughter. It binds them anew during a Lincoln Center performance of "The Tales of Hoffman," where, wordlessly, they patch up their wounds. (Heal? No. Those scabs will always be pickable.).

Recent findings suggest that it would be nice if a movie like that could go toe-to-toe with something on the level of "The Avengers," but there it is. Still, if you only really know Lonergan for his Oscar-winning "Manchester by the Sea," make it a priority to finally watch "Margaret.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber reveals up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

William Gibson is one of the most influential authors in the sci-fi genre. Often credited for pioneering the cyberpunk subgenre, his most seminal novel, Neuromancer, remains a sci-fi masterpiece in 2026. Despite the timelessness and popularity of his literary work, however, his cyberpunk stories and books have hardly been adapted for the screen.

While many video games, movies, and TV indicates have loosely drawn from his work, there are only a handful of direct mainstream adaptations of his stories. Two of these, Johnny Mnemonic and Latest Rose Hotel, premiered in the '90s and struggled to leave their mark. One, titled The Peripheral, premiered on Prime Video in 2022 before being canceled after one season.

Considering the long-standing legacy and influence of William Gibson's work, it is unfortunate that none of his adaptations have worked too well on the screen so far. However, this will soon likely change. Apple TV is now adapting one of William Gibson's most iconic cyberpunk sci-fi books, Neuromancer, which has the potential to become one of the biggest events of the genre in this decade.

Sources indicate that most cyberpunk TV demonstrates and movies focus a little too much on the visual aspect, featuring neon-soaked cityscapes and edgy characters. Prime Video's The Peripheral, on the other hand, truly understood the essence of William Gibson's near-future cyberpunk. In its 2032 timeline, the show features a very familiar, economically broken rural America.

Sources indicate that technology is deeply grafted onto the blue-collar lives of regular people. There are 3-D printed pharmaceuticals, while even veterans with disabilities use military implants called "haptics." The series also reveals its central VR technology as a form of escapism for the main characters who place it in a run-down trailer.

Then comes the show's 2099 timeline where it contrasts 2032's "low lives" with London's high-tech and elite. This is when The Peripheral also introduces "The Jackpot," to reveal the high stakes of its apocalyptic conflict and how humanity's unchecked ambition in the future has pushed civilization to the brink of collapse.

In its 8-episode runtime, Prime Video's The Peripheral did enough to earn more follow-ups and expand its sci-fi vision in season 2. It was a rare adaptation that embraced the hard-edged sci-fi and weirdness of its source material. Unfortunately, despite being promising, its renewal was reversed by Prime Video after SAG-AFTRA and Writers Guild of America's strikes in 2023.

The works of many sci-fi authors, like Philip K. Dick, are not easy to adapt. Yet, Philip K. Dick's stories have already received multiple worthy on-screen adaptations. William Gibson's adaptations, in contrast, have almost been cursed. The ones like Johnny Mnemonic became cult classics, but never achieved mainstream acclaim or success.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, The Peripheral had immense potential, but failed to last beyond one season. After being considered "unfilmable" for quite some time, William Gibson's Neuromancer is finally being adapted by Apple TV. And so far, it looks like the show will finally spell redemption for William Gibson's adaptations.

In a recent development, apple TV's history of bringing challenging adaptations like Isaac Asimov's Foundation to the screen alone is a proof of concept for its ability to successfully translate "unfilmable" sci-fi literature. William Gibson, too, has been directly involved with the show's production, which also heavily favors the adaptation.

Industry observers note that not to mention, after its first trailer, it looks like Apple TV's Neuromancer is not bogging down William Gibson's original vision. If all goes well, the upcoming sci-fi series could become a massive hit and make up for the pitfalls and cancelation of Prime Video's The Peripheral.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that since the starship Enterprise first rolled out its mission to boldly go where no one has gone before in 1966, "Star Trek" has inspired countless things that we've seen in our modern world.
  • It has been revealed that there is, however, one thing inspired by "Star Trek" that seems very unlikely, both for its unusual real-world connection and the fact that it seems to run counter to the franchise's vision of a moneyless, post-scarcity utopia: the McDonald's Happy Meal marketing tie-in.
  • Long before it made it to outer space, the Happy Meal got its start in Guatemala, when a franchisee named Yolanda Fernández de Cofiño came up with the idea of offering kid-sized portions to customers in order to draw in families.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that since the starship Enterprise first rolled out its mission to boldly go where no one has gone before in 1966, "Star Trek" has inspired countless things that we've seen in our modern world. Astronaut Mae Jemison, for example, credited Nichelle Nichols' performance as Lt. Uhura with inspiring her to become the first African-American woman to make it into space. Even the flip phones of the '90s were at least partially inspired by the design of the communicators on the original "Trek.".

It has been revealed that there is, however, one thing inspired by "Star Trek" that seems very unlikely, both for its unusual real-world connection and the fact that it seems to run counter to the franchise's vision of a moneyless, post-scarcity utopia: the McDonald's Happy Meal marketing tie-in. That's right: "Star Trek: The Motion Picture" was the first movie to be featured in a Happy Meal.

Long before it made it to outer space, the Happy Meal got its start in Guatemala, when a franchisee named Yolanda Fernández de Cofiño came up with the idea of offering kid-sized portions to customers in order to draw in families. McDonald's executives liked the idea and hired advertiser Bob Bernstein, who decided to bundle those smaller portions into a box that would feature bright, kid-friendly colors and a small toy to keep the youngsters entertained while mom and dad threw down on their Significant Macs. Thus, the Happy Meal was born, and after being tested in 1977, it rolled out nationwide in 1979.

Sources indicate that needless to say, it was a hit with customers, but the last piece of this familiar fry-scented puzzle would come at the end of the year, when "Star Trek" was revived for the significant screen with the entire main cast of the show returning to their roles. When the film ran over budget during production — not to mention injuries and other problems plaguing the set — Paramount's Vice President of Marketing and Licensing, Dawn Steel, was tasked with figuring out how to cover some of the rapidly expanding costs. She went looking for brand partners, and apparently someone at McDonald's was enough of a Trekkie to go for it. This approach was so successful that it would become almost mandatory for blockbuster movies to have some sort of fast-food tie-in as the years went on, a marketing tactic that would even change the direction of entire franchises, like it did with the infamous "Batman Returns" tie-in.

Sources indicate that looking back, doing a Happy Meal tie-in for "Star Trek: The Motion Picture" was, well, kind of a weird choice. As much as "Trek" had become a cultural touchstone due to the popularity of syndicated re-runs after its original three-season run, the film is a pretty slow, ponderous affair. It's largely about negotiating with a sentient space cloud, punctuated with bits of action like the scene where two members of the ship's crew die screaming for almost a full minute in a transporter accident. It's not a particularly gory or violent movie and there's nothing too objectionable, but it's not exactly "Bambi" — which would get its own Happy Meal tie-in in 1988 — either.

It's especially funny to think about the movie's slow-paced meditations on the unknown and the toll of aging in the context of the Happy Meal itself. Considering that the ad for the Happy Meal involved a Klingon yelling things like "yum-yum" and laughing at the jokes printed on the boxes, they might have given kids a bit of an unrealistic idea of what they were going to get at the movie theater.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that like many comics aimed at children, Charles Schulz's Peanuts doesn't have too many actual villains. It has a number of antagonists, such as Lucy Van Pelt, various other kids, or the impersonal cloud of failure that constantly hangs over Charlie Brown's head, but it's rare to see a genuinely malevolent force in Peanuts — with one exception.

Recent findings suggest that one of Charlie Brown's long-standing hobbies in Peanuts was kite-flying, despite not being very good at it. Whenever he tried it, he invariably got his kite caught in trees and/or himself wrapped up in the kite string. Like every other hobby in Charlie Brown's life, he was devoted to it despite his bad luck.

Recent findings suggest that that hobby eventually introduced Charlie Brown to his nemesis. The Kite-Eating Tree was an otherwise unidentified tree in Charlie Brown's neighborhood that seemed to deliberately grab and eat his kites, to the point where Charlie Brown developed a one-sided rivalry with it.

According to Schulz in the autobiographical collection My Life With Charlie Brown (2010), the inspiration for the Kite-Eating Tree was simply a bit of observational humor. Schulz had noticed that a kite that got stuck in a tree would slowly disappear over the course of several weeks, as wildlife and the elements took their toll. He decided that must've been because the tree was eating the kite, and so the Kite-Eating Tree ended up in Peanuts.

The Kite-Eating Tree was first specifically identified in March 1965, which marked the beginning of a recurring story that would last for the next 30 years.

In many of its appearances, the Kite-Eating Tree doesn't actually do much of anything. In fact, it's noted to have fallen down at one point, but Charlie Brown's subsequent run-ins with the tree suggests that either there's more than one or it's some kind of elected position. Having mentioned that, it’s shown on more than one occasion to be actively devouring its “prey.”.

It has been revealed that the two major Kite-Eating Tree storylines are from the late 1960s and 1970s. One involves Charlie Brown escalating the stakes in the conflict and subsequently having to run from the Environmental Protection Agency, while the other involves Lucy feeding Schroeder's piano to the tree. Both stories were adopted into episodes of the short-lived '80s cartoon The Charlie Brown and Snoopy Show.

In January 1969, Lucy's one-sided obsession with Schroeder reached a boiling point. Fed up with Schroeder's refusal to pay attention to her instead of constantly practicing, she threw his toy piano into the closest tree. Unfortunately, it was the Kite-Eating Tree, which was entirely willing to broaden its diet with a piano. Despite an attempt by Snoopy to rescue the piano, it was soon gone, and Schroeder had to mail-order a replacement.

It has been revealed that the second major Kite-Eating Tree storyline is more surreal, and lasted an unusually long time for a Peanuts arc. On Feb. 25, 1977, Charlie Brown demonstrated an unusual amount of jaw strength when he chose to retaliate against the Kite-Eating Tree. If it was going to bite his kites, he reasoned, he'd just bite it right back, and took quite a piece out of the Tree’s side.

Sources indicate that A few days later, Charlie Brown received a letter from the EPA about the tree. While we're never told what the letter said, Charlie Brown decides to run away from home to escape the charges. Over the next few weeks, he reaches another town, sleeps in a cardboard box, ends up as the upcoming coach of a pee-wee baseball team, and finally gets talked into going home, as the EPA has no case. Besides, the Kite-Eating Tree has since fallen over.

That didn't keep the Kite-Eating Tree from making future appearances, but it was primarily a one-joke wonder for most of the rest of Peanuts' run.

Its final appearance came in 1995, when Charlie Brown's attempt to teach Rerun how to fly a kite ended in disaster. Charlie Brown would continue to unsuccessfully fly kites from time to time until March 1999, but the Tree was out of the picture for good.

Recent findings suggest that with one last kite for the road, the Kite-Eating Tree was never seen again, but one must assume that it's still out there somewhere. Waiting. Hungering for fresh kites. Annoyed that kids don't really seem to fly kites as much as they used to.

💡 Key Takeaways
