📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in 1972, Walter Hill was a young screenwriter with just one produced movie (“Hickey & Boggs”) behind him when he scored an enviable gig: adapting Jim Thompson’s tough-as-nails crime novel “The Getaway” for actor/producer Steve McQueen (then one of the biggest movie stars in the world) and director Sam Peckinpah (then, as now, one of the greatest directors who ever lived). On Wednesday night, Hill spoke before a packed screening at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and looked back on the movie that jump-started not only his screenwriting endeavors, but a directing career that would ultimately include classics like “The Warriors,” “48hrs.,” and “Streets of Fire.” Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

“The Getaway” screened as part of the museum’s “Branch Selects” series, in which the Academy’s various branches program films they feel exemplify their crafts. “The Getaway” was, appropriately enough, selected by the writers branch, and screenwriter and Academy Governor Larry Karaszewski was on hand to introduce the movie and moderate the pre-screening discussion with Hill. Karaszewski, a longtime “Getaway” enthusiast who carried newspaper ads from the movie around in his wallet when he was 10 years old, pointed out that Hill changed the entire architecture of screenwriting when he burst onto the scene in the early 1970s.

“ Walter, right off the bat, changed the art of screenwriting,” Karaszewski said. “We have an award show here at the Oscars called the Sci-Tech Awards, where they give awards to things that silently change the industry and advance them into the future. I really feel that Walter Hill did that in screenwriting, but it wasn’t a technical advancement. It was a literary advancement. He changed what a page should look like as a screenplay and what it could feel like to read it.” Karaszewski went on to illustrate his point by projecting pages from Robert Bolt’s “Doctor Zhivago” screenplay and Walter Hill’s “Hard Times” side by side on the screen.

In a recent development, “You don’t even have to read [Bolt’s script], just look at it,” Karaszewski remarked, pointing out the dense blocks of words compared to Hill’s lean, spare page. “You’re looking at monoliths. It’s dense, and there are camera moves and references to things you would never see on screen. Walter Hill taught screenwriters that you can strip all that away. You can still direct on the page, but not by calling for specific camera movements — just by saying what you’re seeing. Walter’s scripts are made out of short sentences and white space. He looked at the placement of each line as part of the storytelling. He turned the carriage return into an art form.”.

According to recent reports, as Karaszewski welcomed Hill to the stage, he pointed out that “The Getaway” — a smart, terse tale of a couple (Steve McQueen and Ali MacGraw) on the run after their involvement in a botched bank robbery — represented the emergence of Hill’s developing voice. “You’ll already see the beginnings of that remarkable style, the economy, the precision, the sense that every line is pushing you toward the next image.” Yet, as Hill revealed in his lively conversation with Karaszewski, the ruthless efficiency of the pacing and the concentrated emotional impact of “The Getaway” were not easily arrived at.

“I think it’s much harder to adapt than it is to write an original, which is the reverse of the normal theory,” Hill said. “With an original, it’s just you at your desk with the typewriter or pen. When you’re adapting, that almost always means that somebody else owns it, so you’re not simply writing based on your own opinions about what should be in and what should be out, but there’s the producer’s opinion, and the studio’s, and the actor’s. There were all these political currents that one had to navigate.”.

One such political current came from megastar McQueen, who didn’t interfere much with Hill’s writing but did have one caveat that amused the screenwriter. “He wanted to play a reasonably sympathetic outlaw,” Hill noted. “That was not in the Thompson sensibility. So we already had a disparity, but the producer wanted to keep Steve happy.”.

“The Getaway” began as an assignment not for Peckinpah, but for Peter Bogdanovich, who was white-hot coming off of successes like “The Last Picture Show” and “What’s Up, Doc?” Bogdanovich didn’t last long, however, given his clashes with McQueen and McQueen’s power as the film‘s star. “I couldn’t imagine two more diverse sensibilities than Steve and Peter,” Hill stated, noting that he had his own disagreements with Bogdanovich over the movie’s tone but wasn’t in a position to argue. “You’ve got to remember, I was nobody. I had one screen credit. And these were substantial players.”.

Sources indicate that the major players included not only Bogdanovich and McQueen, but MacGraw, hot off of the smash hit “Love Story.” MacGraw was pushed into the movie by her husband, Paramount studio chief Robert Evans, which Hill found amusing given the way everything played out. “I’m going to tread lightly here,” Hill mentioned of the behind-the-scenes melodrama involving MacGraw leaving Evans when she fell in love with McQueen. “When the material was optioned and I was hired, Bob saw the movie as a fabulous idea for Steve and Ali. It didn’t work out so well for him.”.

Industry observers note that after Bogdanovich and McQueen butted heads, Bogdanovich was let go and Peckinpah, who McQueen had enjoyed working with on “Junior Bonner,” came in to take his place. “We were very lucky to get such a talented guy, obviously,” Hill noted. “I thought of him then and I think of him now as one of the great directors with a very unique sensibility. I was very privileged to work with him — which doesn’t mean he and I agreed about everything.”.

Recent findings suggest that hill’s biggest disagreement with Peckinpah had to do with a scene in which MacGraw’s character considered killing McQueen before turning the gun on his nemesis — and the man with whom MacGraw had gone to bed to secure McQueen’s early release from prison. This was a scene carried over from the book, which was darker and more paranoid than what made it to the screen given McQueen’s mandate that he be sympathetic. Hill felt that the moment no longer worked now that the relationship between McQueen and MacGraw was softer and more relatable in the novel.

Sources indicate that “I thought that for the movie we were trying to make, you might forgive your wife for sleeping with a bad man to do a very good thing for you,” Hill stated. “That seemed to be to be conceivable. But if your wife fell into cahoots with the bad guy and actually was thinking about killing you and actually turned the gun on you before she decided to shoot the other guy…this did not track for me. But this is the screenwriter’s dilemma: you either talk the director into your point of view, or you make the change that he wants — or somebody else will. Those are your choices.”.

Sources indicate that hill lost the argument but liked the movie Peckinpah made in the end. “He staged it beautifully,” Hill remarked. “He shot it beautifully. It’s got one of Steve’s best performances. And the movie turned out to be his greatest hit. He used to call me every once in a while after I became a director and say, ‘Write me another one.'” Ironically, it was the success of “The Getaway” that put Hill in a position where didn’t have to write for other directors anymore.

“Larry Gordon had a producing deal to make low-budget movies at Columbia,” Hill said. “He would give young writers a chance to direct, because he said, ‘Even if they’re no good as directors, at least we’ll get a good script. Most of the directors I’m working with aren’t any good anyway.'” Gordon gave Hill the opportunity to direct “Hard Times,” and the rest was history. Aside from kicking off Hill’s directing career, the collaboration became the first of many between the two men. “He’s a wonderful guy and a wonderful producer.”.

Now in his 80s, Hill continues to write and direct (his last film was the exquisite character-driven Western “Dead for a Dollar“), plying his trade in the world of graphic novels in between film projects. “I’ve had four of them published in France,” Hill said, joking that the only one published in America was “the least good of them,” but promising another one on the way. “You’ve got to keep your hand in somehow.”.

There is no new episode of "SNL" on November 21, 2026.

5 Essential Classic Books for Beginners

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that at any given moment, Scott Simone has at least three books jockeying for his attention.
  • He’s spent so much time in book shops over the years he is, to his wife’s chagrin, continuing to build a library that doesn’t quite respect the dimensions of the apartment meant to contain it.
  • If you don't want someone to read a book, tell them it’s a classic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that at any given moment, Scott Simone has at least three books jockeying for his attention. He’ll never turn down a campus novel with a literary bent, nor will he hesitate to add yet another mystery to his Leaning Tower of Pisa-inspired to-be-read pile — which is built upon the bedrocks of too many short story collections, how-are-these-real true crime books, and classics waiting to be cracked open again. Topics that have him ripping through pages the fastest include closed-circle murders, unhappy professors, life-questioning philosophical deep dives, so long as they feature sharp sentences, a dark sense of humor, and at least a little malice.

He’s spent so much time in book shops over the years he is, to his wife’s chagrin, continuing to build a library that doesn’t quite respect the dimensions of the apartment meant to contain it.

If you don't want someone to read a book, tell them it’s a classic. Tell them that it changed literature. Tell them how generations of writers have tried and failed to reproduce it. Tell them no bookshelf is complete without it. Now you’ve made reading a chore. It’s homework. We seem more interested in what these books represent than what's actually between their covers. But none of that tells you whether you'll enjoy spending an afternoon with one.

Recent findings suggest that and God help you if you don't enjoy one. Give up on a modern novel halfway through, and it's simply not for you. Put down a classic, and feel the judgment pour. Somebody will come along to explain what you did wrong. Perhaps you didn't understand the historical context. Maybe you missed the symbolism. Give it another go in 10 years, when you're older and a little wiser. Sometimes that's fair. But we've developed a habit of treating difficulty as a mark of greatness, as though the more you struggle through a book, the more worthwhile the experience. And that's a shame. These were novels — funny, exciting, full of people behaving appallingly — long before they became monuments to literature. And perhaps the best way to appreciate their greatness is to remember what made them worth reading in the first place.

If you think 19th-century literature is a slog, Jane Austen would like a word. And in all likelihood, it'll be a funny one. Because Austen knows how to bring the humor, especially when she's eviscerating the types of people who tend to make fools of themselves. Pride and Prejudice rotates a cast of such characters right into her firing line. There's Mrs. Bennet, who's basically willing to marry off her five daughters to whichever eligible bachelors wander into the neighborhood. There's Mr. Collins, a man so impressed with himself he has no doubt everyone else must be, too. And then there's Elizabeth Bennet, who's clever enough to recognize everyone else's shortcomings, but isn't quite so perceptive when it comes to her own. The best part: You don't need to know much about Regency England to appreciate any of this. Snobs, bores, and people who think far too highly of themselves were plentiful two centuries ago, and Austen brings them hilariously to life.

The romance is familiar enough, too. Elizabeth and the wealthy-but-insufferable Mr. Darcy spend an awful lot of time misunderstanding one another, taking offense at perfectly innocent remarks, and refusing to admit when they've been wrong. It's not so far removed from a modern romantic comedy, though there's more at stake than a few bruised egos. Money and social standing dictate much of what these people can and can't do, especially when it comes to marriage. For Elizabeth and her sisters, finding a suitable husband is as much a matter of financial security as it is romance. Yes, the language does take some getting used to, and polite society and all its rules can seem ridiculous. But Austen thought plenty of them were ridiculous, too, and she's more than happy to have a little fun at their expense.

It has been revealed that not every literary classic takes a fortnight to actually get going. Case in point: Around the World in Eighty Days. Jules Verne takes a simple premise, launches out of the gates with it, and never really slows his pace. Which can't exactly be remarked for Phileas Fogg, an English gentleman who seems a little too obsessed with punctuality. Yet he wagers £20,000 that he can travel around the globe in 80 days. This being 1872 and all, a time when travel involved nothing more than a few steamships and trains, it's an outrageous proposition. But that's all the setup Verne needs. There's no sprawling cast to keep track of and no complicated backstory to untangle. There's simply a man and a deadline — and a ridiculous number of obstacles standing between the two.

It has been revealed that fogg, mind you, is hardly the sort of man you'd expect to go gallivanting around the world. He's a creature of habit, so wedded to his daily routine that you'd think the slightest disruption would send him into a fit. However, Verne seems determined to test just how much the man can take. A train is missed. A connection falls through. An itinerary becomes useless. Somehow, Fogg takes it all in stride, with the composure of a man who's been told his dinner reservation has been pushed back 15 minutes. His French valet, Passepartout, isn't so accommodating, and watching him fret while his employer barely bats an eye is half the fun. And Verne makes us fret along with him. A delayed departure becomes genuinely suspenseful. Some of the novel's attitudes toward the people and places encountered along the way are decidedly of their time; but Verne's talent for turning a simple journey into one calamity after another hasn't aged much at all.

Not every difficult subject makes for a difficult book. Leo Tolstoy takes on death and regret. He delves into the despair of a life wasted in The Death of Ivan Ilyich, and he manages it in about 100 pages. The writing is surprisingly straightforward, the cast is small, and there's hardly any plot to untangle. We learn that Ivan, a Russian judge, has died before we've even had a chance to meet the man. So there's no great mystery about where this is headed. What concerns Tolstoy is how Ivan got there, and why a man who's done just about everything expected of him finds himself so unprepared for the end. It's heavy stuff, sure. But you don't need a philosophy degree or much knowledge of 19th-century Russia to understand what Tolstoy's getting at.

Sources indicate that tolstoy has a wicked sense of humor, which helps. Ivan's colleagues hear that he's died and immediately start calculating what it might mean for their careers. His funeral is treated as an inconvenience, something to get through before going about life. Ivan himself hasn't exactly spent his years pursuing a life of great meaning. He's been too busy climbing the social ladder and worrying about what people might think of him. Then he gets sick, and suddenly none of it seems worth much. Worse still, the people around him would sooner carry on pretending everything is fine than acknowledge what's happening to him. Tolstoy has plenty of fun exposing all this vanity and self-importance.

Industry observers note that toni Collette and Kit Harington are shooting a latest Miss Marple and 20th Century has several more Christies in development, so the drawing room is busier than it has been in decades. Here is which of them you are, and the case for yours being the best.

Order, method, and a quiet confidence that you are the cleverest person present. Poirot is a retired Belgian police officer who solves murders by sitting still and thinking, and who is vain enough to make the reveal a performance every single time.

Sources indicate that people tell you things because they cannot imagine you being a threat. Marple solves murders by comparing everybody to somebody she once knew in St Mary Mead, which sounds like a joke until you notice it works every time, because human beings are not as original as they think.

Industry observers note that you have far too many ideas and roughly a fifth of them are excellent. Ariadne Oliver is a successful crime novelist who is sick of her famous foreign detective and keeps saying so, which is Christie writing about Christie and getting away with it completely.

According to recent reports, you are steady, decent and the reason the difficult genius has anybody at all. Hastings narrates the early Poirot novels, misses most of the clues, and is the only character in the books that Poirot is unambiguously fond of, which tells you what he is really for.

You can spend eons trying to decipher Franz Kafka. Literary scholars have been at it for more than a century. But The Metamorphosis doesn't require much deciphering to enjoy. Kafka gives us the whole ridiculous premise in his opening sentence: Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman, wakes up as an enormous insect. Gregor's reaction is almost as absurd as the transformation itself. He's worried about being late for work. He's missed his train, his boss is going to be furious, and his family needs the money. The man's no longer human, and he's fretting about how he'll explain his absence to his employer. It's horribly funny, especially because the thinking behind it isn't all that difficult to recognize.

According to recent reports, kafka's joke gets considerably darker as the story goes on. Gregor has spent years working to support his parents and sister, putting their needs ahead of his own. Now that he's the one who needs looking after, the family isn't exactly enthusiastic to act in kind. His sister initially takes pity on him. His father can barely stand the sight of him. Eventually, everyone gets a bit sick and tired of having an enormous insect in their house. All the while, Gregor seems more concerned about becoming a burden than he does about his own misery. It's an awful arrangement, but one that doesn't take much imagination to understand.

Nella Larsen proves you don't need a murder or mayhem for a gripping psychological thriller. She managed to do so with an old friendship and a few uncomfortable conversations. Passing is barely 150 pages, but Larsen packs enough suspicion and intrigue to fill hundreds more. It centers on two Black women, Irene Redfield and Clare Kendry, childhood friends who've taken very different paths in life. Clare passes as white, even marrying a wealthy white man who’d never guess she's Black. Odd, considering he's so viciously racist. On the other hand, Irene has built a comfortable life in Harlem, and she knows just how badly Clare's deception could end. But when the two reconnect, she can't bring herself to stay away.

There's plenty to worry about, but it's the conversations between Irene and Clare that make the novel so fraught. Larsen lets Irene do much of the interpreting for us, and we fall into the habit of taking her word for it. Clare is reckless. Clare craves attention. Clare is putting everyone at risk. And perhaps she's right about all of it. But the more we learn about Irene, the harder it becomes to separate genuine concern from jealousy and resentment. Larsen is great at making us suspicious of someone without giving us much evidence against them. So much so that an ordinary conversation can seem loaded with meaning, a perfectly innocent remark like a veiled threat. And so we find ourselves scrutinizing every little exchange, wondering who's being truthful and who's got something to hide.

It is more cost-efficient to find 100 Americans and bring them to Ireland and shoot the game show in Ireland than it is to shoot in the soundstages [on the Fox lot] right outside the window of the offices where we’re trying to figure out what we’re going to do next season.

Yeah, this really illustrates the rough situation in LA right now. When I looked deeper into it, I found out that there are a few factors that probably played into The Floor deciding to go to Ireland rather than stay in Los Angeles. One is the rigid labor regulations in Los Angeles that just don’t apply in Ireland. Another is how much more expensive it would be for the production to board the one hundred contestants during the shoots. And then, there’s the competitive tax incentives Ireland has in place to encourage productions to be there. Lowe continued with these words:.

There’s a new California initiative that did pass to help bring production back into LA. And then, there's also a national one that people are talking about. But, that would still only make it competitive with some of the other [markets]. I mean, it’s 40% less expensive, 40. It’s a lot of money.

It sounds like The Floor just wouldn’t be able to exist if it were shot in Los Angeles. There are a number of TV indicates that at the moment shoot in the City of Angels, like Dancing With The Stars, The Pitt, The Rookie, 911, Shrinking and Abbott Elementary, and some incentives in California are starting to help repair the market. However, as Lowe also shared while on Mostly Sheenius, there’s a long way to go before it becomes cost-efficient again. As he put it:.

It is definitely trending up, but it is trending up from the basement of where it used to be.

Tons of Los Angeles TV reveals recently moved to new locations, such as Shark Tank and American Idol moving to Atlanta and The Masked Singer to New Jersey. It’s also been reported lately (per Deadline) that America’s Got Talent is scouting a new home outside of its longtime home in Pasadena, California.

In a recent development, the Floor airs latest episodes on Wednesdays (with the finale airing on December 2). If you’re looking to catch up on the new season, you can do so now with either a Disney+ subscription and/or a Hulu subscription. Lowe’s explanation of why The Floor shoots in Ireland kind of blows my mind, but as a Los Angeles resident, I totally see how expensive it is over here, too. Hopefully some of these incentives will change things because so much of the workforce over here relies on the entertainment industry.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.
  • Industry observers note that at this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two.
  • Recent findings suggest that more concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Sumerian Pictures will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20, with a wide release to follow on Friday, December 4.].

Industry observers note that at this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two. Not just in terms of the quality of her films — impeccably crafted fever dreams of very different stripes and horrifyingly similar themes — but in how these films make the viewer feel.

Recent findings suggest that more concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Recent findings suggest that the word that comes to mind when watching a de Araújo feature is heartsick. That applies to the feeling bestowed on both the audience and her characters (the good guys and the bad guys). While her first film, the unrelenting “Soft & Quiet,” was cleverly designed to appear as if it was shot in a single real-time take, her sophomore feature is more about the steady accumulation of dread. The heroines of “Soft & Quiet” recognize what they are dealing with almost immediately (the force of the evil that is bent on destroying them is what’s surprises most), but the star at the center of “Josephine” is not just wounded by the sickness that suddenly infiltrates her young life, but her complete lack of understanding about what is happening to her and why.

In both films, it’s not just bad deeds that upends everyday lives, it’s real evil, actual monsters, perversions that don’t only show up in a movie screen. That’s true terror.

Based loosely on an experience de Araújo, who both wrote and directed the film, experienced as a child, “Josephine” initially lulls us into a false sense of safety. It’s early morning in San Francisco, and fledgling soccer star Josephine (Mason Reeves, riveting in her first role) is getting ready for a run with her devoted dad Damien (Channing Tatum, bringing incredible girl-dad energy to the role). It’s something the pair do every Sunday morning: get up early to watch Premier League football, run through a woodsy neighboring park, and kick the ball around.

It has been revealed that for her second film, de Araújo leans less on clever camera tricks, though she and cinematographer Greta Zozula occasionally put us in Josephine’s own perspective, shooting as if we are looking through the eight-year-old’s eyes. As with “Soft & Quiet,” the gimmick works, grounding us in Josephine’s world and immersing us, if briefly, in what the world looks like from her vantage. Jo-Jo, as her dad calls her, is plucky and fun and filled with energy, so when she briefly zips ahead of her dad while on their run through Golden Gate Park, it just seems like everyday high-jinks.

But when the path forks (about as heavy-handed a metaphor as de Araújo will ever employ), Josephine goes to the left, while Damien goes to the right. What she finds there will forever alter the course of her life, and set “Josephine” off on a heart-wrenching journey with no easy answers. Curious and watchful, Josephine ducks behind a tree when she sees a woman (Syra McCarthy) running into a public bathroom at the bottom of a scrubby hill, and she sinks even further down when a young man (a bone-chilling Philip Ettinger) follows the unknown woman into the tiny building.

According to recent reports, de Araújo’s approach to portraying on-screen violence only furthers that heartsick feeling: straightforward, unsparing, and absolutely devoid of any possibility of being compared to “torture porn.” What we see, what Josephine sees, is something no person should ever witness or experience. And that’s the root of the film’s power: how do we talk about things that we should not have words for?

When Damien arrives on the scene, it kicks off what will become one of Tatum’s best performances yet, a deep-feeling and heartbreaking exploration of layers of emotional unease. Damien does everything “right,” ensuring both Josephine and the woman are safe, chasing after the assailant, calling the cops, a neat little checklist of “how to handle an emergency.” And yet, the damage has already been done. There will be more to come.

It has been revealed that even when Josephine begins to seek out answers to what she’s seen (snatching her mom’s phone to search “raip,” reeling at what she discovers), it’s impossible to make sense of everything. There are things to fear she never even know existed, and the deep-seated powerlessness that overtakes her causes her to act out in chilling and increasingly volatile ways. Her parents’ reactions don’t help: her exceedingly calm mother Claire (Gemma Chan, thrilling as a character just barely holding it together) wants her to see a therapist now, her more action-oriented dad is eager to put her into self-defense classes. The mixed messages both give off (to say nothing of their own barely concealed terror) do little to help Josephine, who soon becomes someone almost entirely different than the care-free kid she just was.

According to recent reports, she also picks up a new friend: Ettinger begins to appear to her, a literal haunting figure, never saying a word, yet barging into nearly every moment of Josephine’s already upended life. It’s the sort of choice another filmmaker fight fill tricksy or silly, but that de Araújo delivers with the maximum of impact. And that we, like Josephine and only Josephine, can see him only furthers our immersion into her world. It almost goes beyond empathy.

Sources indicate that josephine’s steadily unfolding breakdown is only compounded by the arrival of yet another situation no eight-year-old should ever have to encounter: handling the messy investigation of the crime itself. How she might help (or not) drives one more wedge between Josephine and her parents, who all have a different take on what the “right” thing to do is.

Sources indicate that if these questions sound heady and heavy, they are, but de Araújo’s masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability. The monsters are here, they are real, and they’re coming.

“Josephine” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

DC's Next Batman Was Never Going To Be Nightwing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On the surface, Dick Grayson's Nightwing may seem like an obvious choice to one day succeed Batman and don the cape and cowl.
  • In the past, Dick Grayson had indeed filled in as Batman in Bruce Wayne's absence.
  • According to recent reports, ever since he left Robin behind, Dick's evolution into Nightwing has long been punctuated by the desire to be more than Batman and step out of his shadow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the surface, Dick Grayson's Nightwing may seem like an obvious choice to one day succeed Batman and don the cape and cowl. After all, he was The Dark Knight's very first Robin and oldest adopted son. However, DC Comics has spent quite some time establishing a much different trajectory for Grayson, while setting up someone else entirely to one day become the next Caped Crusader.

In the past, Dick Grayson had indeed filled in as Batman in Bruce Wayne's absence. However, it's one thing to become a temporary Dark Knight or for the comics to showcase an alt-reality "What If?" type scenario (see DC K.O. Knightfight), and quite another to suggest that Nightwing will one day become a full-time Batman for the foreseeable future. That's never going to be in the cards for several reasons.

According to recent reports, ever since he left Robin behind, Dick's evolution into Nightwing has long been punctuated by the desire to be more than Batman and step out of his shadow. Conversely, DC Comics clearly has someone else in mind to become the next Batman, and he's already been wearing the cape and cowl: Jace Fox.

According to recent reports, dick Grayson has successfully taken over as Batman before, most notably after Bruce Wayne's apparent death in Final Crisis. This era saw Dick becoming a newly introduced Batman alongside Damian Wayne as his Robin in the critically acclaimed Batman and Robin run. As such, it's been proven that Dick can and has become The Dark Knight when needed (but that doesn't mean he should long-term).

When he left his role as Robin behind, Dick Grayson's decision to become Nightwing was all about creating a newly introduced identity all his own, beyond Bruce. This included his move to Gotham's sister city of Blüdhaven. In the several years that have followed, Dick has become an A-list DC hero in his own right in the modern era, leading the Titans and protecting his own city without needing Batman's name or reputation.

According to recent reports, perhaps even more importantly, Bruce himself has indicated that he wants something far better for his eldest son (and all his sons) than simply becoming another Batman in his stead. Likewise, Dick Grayson has retained so much more of his optimism and brightness, choosing to move past his own parents' deaths rather than Bruce and his ongoing struggle to do just that.

Rather than asking him to ever take his place full-time, Bruce Wayne has every reason to want Dick to continue being Nightwing and prove that the next generation can become something greater than Batman himself. He already knows (and has remarked) that Dick is a far greater hero as Nightwing than he'll ever be as Batman. As such, wanting Dick to become Batman would undermine several years of development and crucial storytelling for both characters and their relationship.

Timothy "Jace" Fox, the estranged son of Lucius Fox, is a far more interesting possibility. First introduced as the next Batman in DC's Future State initiative, Jace received a proper present-day origin in The Next Batman: Second Son, exploring his complicated history and years away from his family. When he came back to Gotham, Jace chose to take up Batman's mantle, using advanced armor to fight as a secondary Dark Knight before eventually moving to Fresh York City.

Sources indicate that as seen in I Am Batman, the series explored what a new character could do with the mantle of The Dark Knight outside Gotham itself. At the same time, Jace's connection to Lucius still kept him connected to many of the resources associated with Bruce Wayne's crusade.

Industry observers note that keeping that in mind, the upcoming Batman: Reign of Assassins series is particularly exciting. Releasing in 2027, the five-matter series reunites writer John Ridley and artist Olivier Coipel, bringing Jace and Bruce together for their first true ongoing team-up, which should no doubt provide some brand-new explorations into their dynamics as simultaneous Batmen.

All things considered, DC Comics absolutely intends to use Jace to continue examining what the Batman legacy looks like in a upcoming generation, and it will be SO much better than Dick Grayson ever becoming a permanent next Dark Knight.

Batman: Reign of Assassins #1 is available February 27 from DC Comics.

#51328. 58 Years Later, Captain Kirk's Best Star Trek Quote Is the Greatest Line in Sci-Fi History

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (931 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Polygon ↗ Open Full Page

58 Years Later, Captain Kirk's Best Star Trek Quote Is the Greatest Line in Sci-Fi History

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (931 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some lines of dialogue become so famous they stop belonging to the movies and TV indicates that produced them.
  • Star Trek: The Original Series has plenty of those.
  • But if I could only pick one line to represent everything Star Trek stands for, it would be four simple words spoken by Captain James T.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some lines of dialogue become so famous they stop belonging to the movies and TV indicates that produced them. “May the Force be with you.” “I’ll be back.” “You're gonna need a bigger boat.” You don't need to know the context. The words have long since transcended their original context and permeated the pop culture zeitgeist.

Star Trek: The Original Series has plenty of those. Spock’s wish that everyone to “Live long and prosper” is arguably the franchise's signature phrase. He also turned the simple word “fascinating” into a catchphrase simply by raising one eyebrow before saying it. Dr. McCoy (DeForest Kelley) spent three seasons reminding everyone, “I'm a doctor, not a…” and, at least in our collective memory declaring, “He's dead, Jim” while standing over the latest redshirt who wandered a little too far from the landing party.

But if I could only pick one line to represent everything Star Trek stands for, it would be four simple words spoken by Captain James T. Kirk (William Shatner) halfway through “Return to Tomorrow," the 20th episode of season 2:.

Industry observers note that on the surface, it doesn't seem like an obvious choice. It's not printed on T-shirts nearly as often as “live long and prosper.” It isn't endlessly quoted by people who have never watched an episode of Star Trek. And unlike “beam me up, Scotty,” it never became part of the broader pop culture vocabulary. But that's exactly why it's the best quote. It doesn't just capture Kirk. It captures the entire philosophy of Star Trek.

First broadcast on Feb. 9, 1968, the episode “Return to Tomorrow” finds the Enterprise answering a mysterious distress call from a dead planet. There, Kirk and his crew discover Sargon, one of three survivors of an ancient civilization that has existed as beings of pure energy for half a million years. Sargon asks Kirk, Spock (Leonard Nimoy), and Dr. Ann Mulhall (Diana Muldaur) to temporarily surrender their bodies so he, his wife Thalassa, and the ambitious Henoch can build android bodies and begin life again. Dr. McCoy believes the aliens are manipulating them. Kirk believes the chance to learn from a civilization hundreds of thousands of years more advanced than humanity is worth the danger.

According to recent reports, the episode also marks the first of three Star Trek appearances by Diana Muldaur. She plays Dr. Ann Mulhall here before returning as Miranda Jones in the third season episode “Is There in Truth No Beauty?” Years later, she'd become a series regular on Star Trek: The Next Generation as Dr. Katherine Pulaski. “Return to Tomorrow” is also a fun piece of Trek trivia because it's one of the times Spock describes Sargon as “pure energy,” a phrase longtime fans immediately recognize.

Faced with allowing unimaginably powerful aliens to occupy the bodies of his crew, Kirk doesn't issue an order. He makes an argument and reminds his crew that every leap forward in human history required someone willing to embrace uncertainty.

"They used to say if man could fly, he'd have wings," Kirk says. "But he did fly. He discovered he had to." He likens Sargon's offer to humanity's own journey from the Moon to Mars and eventually the stars, arguing that the potential for knowledge outweighs the danger. Only then does he arrive at the four words that define both the captain and the franchise. Those four words explain Kirk better than decades of pop-culture impressions ever could.

Sources indicate that for years, pop culture has reduced Kirk to an oversimplified caricature: the swaggering captain who punches first, flirts with every alien woman he meets, and somehow loses his shirt during every other away mission. The real Kirk is far more thoughtful than that. He takes risks, certainly, but not because he enjoys gambling. He takes them because he believes some opportunities are too notable to ignore.

It has been revealed that there's a world of difference between being reckless and accepting risk in pursuit of discovery. Kirk isn't arguing that danger is exciting. He's arguing that progress is impossible without it.

Sources indicate that more importantly, he's explaining what separates Starfleet from almost every other organization. Plenty of fictional explorers travel because they're ordered to. Others do it for conquest, profit, or survival. Starfleet goes because knowledge itself is worth pursuing.

It has been revealed that that's why I think this quote is even more meaningful than the famous opening narration about boldly going where no one has gone before. The opening tells us what the Enterprise does. This one explains why.

It has been revealed that the timing of the episode makes the speech even more remarkable. “Return to Tomorrow” aired in early 1968, roughly 17 months before Apollo 11 landed on the Moon. America was still trying to prove humans could successfully reach another world, and Star Trek was already imagining the next step beyond that. Kirk's speech places the Enterprise in the same lineage as every explorer who came before it, suggesting humanity's future won't be built by playing it safe.

That idea has become the beating heart of Star Trek. Optimism, in the Star Trek universe, has never meant believing everything will work out. It means believing the unknown is worth facing anyway.

Industry observers note that there are more famous quotes in The Original Series. There are funnier ones. There are certainly more quotable ones. But no other line distills what Star Trek has always been trying to say better than four words Kirk spoke nearly 60 years ago: “Risk is our business.”.

5 Actors Who Should Play M In Robert Pattinson's James Bond Movies

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the next era of the "James Bond" film franchise is finally taking shape.
  • In a recent development, historically, this has been the one they call M.
  • Director Denis Villeneuve also has to find an actor to play the villain in Pattinson's "James Bond" movie, but M is a longer commitment, a multi-picture deal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the next era of the "James Bond" film franchise is finally taking shape. After years of wondering who will be suiting up as our fresh 007, Robert Pattinson has officially been cast as the next James Bond, taking over for Daniel Craig following his final entry with "No Time to Die," which came out way back in 2021. A lot has happened since then, including Amazon buying the rights to the property. Now, with a new lead actor in place, it's time to get the rest of the pieces of the puzzle locked in. That includes finding Bond's boss.

In a recent development, historically, this has been the one they call M. Originally portrayed by Bernard Lee in the earliest Bond films, the codename given to the person behind the significant desk at MI6 is an important one, as they head up the 00 program. Thus, M is the one who gives Bond his assignments and, at times, even helps him out in the field. It's an important role, one that has been played by the likes of Dame Judi Dench and Oscar-nominee Ralph Fiennes.

There's much to be done. Director Denis Villeneuve also has to find an actor to play the villain in Pattinson's "James Bond" movie, but M is a longer commitment, a multi-picture deal. It's a massive responsibility. So, who should play the role alongside Pattinson? Who should be the one to help guide 007 through his next several missions for her majesty's secret service?

Recent findings suggest that we're going to go over a handful of options, ranging from very obvious to unlikely yet intriguing. Let's get into it.

Industry observers note that "The amount of time I have wanted to be M. I'm not sure who I need to call...".

In a recent development, those are the words of Olivia Colman speaking to British Vogue in 2023. She wants the role. She's very well qualified for the role. If everyone wants to make this easy, why not just offer her the role? Sometimes, the easiest answer is also a very good answer. That not every actor who campaigns openly for a role should get it, but we're not just talking about any old actor here.

Colman is responsible for one of the most shocking Oscars upsets of all time when she took home Best Actress for "The Favourite." But it was more shocking because the Academy recognized Colman's impressive work over the rest of the pack. Ever since, she's been on a tear, turning in outstanding performances in everything from "The Lost Daughter" to "Paddington in Peru." Heck, she even ate up some screen time in Marvel's otherwise very disappointing series "Secret Invasion.".

It has been revealed that but Colman has been doing it at a very high level for years, long before she won an Oscar. "Hot Fuzz," "The Iron Lady," "Broadchurch." You name it, Colman is one of the best parts of everything she's in. Beyond that, she could bring both a seriousness to the role of M, which is required, while at the same time allowing for a playful dynamic with Bond. Colman feels like a slam dunk. It just so happens that the person campaigning for the role is very much right for the role. That's not always the case.

If Denis Villeneuve or Amazon want to go with a distinguished, male British actor who could be older and wiser than Robert Pattinson's Bond, one capable of being both convincingly stern and charming, Colin Firth is the man. An Oscar-winning actor who is almost too easy to picture sitting at a big desk behind a padded burgundy door, this is another "the obvious choice can also be the right choice" pick.

We have an actor here capable of delivering exposition, as M often has to, in a way that would be entertaining, as Firth could read the phone book and it would be engaging. But let's not forget that Firth politely destroyed fools in "Kingsman: The Secret Service," too, and that movie owes a lot to the "James Bond" franchise. What's more, it proved that Firth looks absolutely fantastic in an expensive suit, an important quality of a good M.

Recent findings suggest that his resume speaks for itself. "A Single Man," "The King's Speech," and even "Mamma Mia!" prove that Firth is one of the finest actors of the last 30 years. There's zero question as to whether or not he's qualified to be M. So, it begs the question: Is he right for M? If we're looking to address that question in the traditional sense, then the answer is a resounding yes. The shoe fits and it fits well. Simple as that.

If it weren't for Judi Dench playing M so damn well for so damn long, we might have to have the utterly irritating "let's gender-swap M" conversation. Fortunately, that's not the world we live in. Bearing that in mind, it's going to be damn hard for anyone to argue against Tilda Swinton bossing around Robert Pattinson while dressed to the nines. What's not to like about that?

Swinton won a Best Supporting Actress Oscar for "Michael Clayton" so, much like many of the other performers on that list, she's Oscar-caliber. That almost feels like a must for M. Setting that aside, Swinton brings a domineering, powerful quality to so many of her best roles. Even so, she's a bit of a chameleon, which is partially what would make her an interesting M. It's not hard to imagine her playing an MI6 agent who used to work in the field before taking a desk job, yet she still has that darkness behind her eyes from yesteryear.

Oddly, it's Swinton's transformation into the Ancient One" in "Doctor Strange" that might make the best case here. She can do powerful yet quiet without having to be at the center of the action, and she can absolutely handle being a part of a giant, globally popular franchise. Really, there's nothing this role requires that she couldn't do, seemingly with ease.

Some might argue Swinton would be better as a "Bond" villain. That certainly wouldn't upset me, but it might be subverting expectations a bit to have her as Bond's buttoned-up boss. She could also help bring something fresh to the role for this latest era.

And now we arrive at the most obvious answer. Does that make it the wrong answer? Using history as our guide, absolutely not. Ralph Fiennes made his entry into the "James Bond" franchise in 2012's "Skyfall" before fully taking over as M in "Spectre" following the death of Judi Dench's M. (May she rest in peace.) So, why replace a perfectly great actor in the role if we don't have to?

Let's not forget that the "James Bond" franchise is notorious for bringing actors back in roles even after reboots. Dench as M for both Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig's Bonds. Desmond Llewelyn was Q for every Bond except Craig. That's the nature of the beast as it exists. If Amazon doesn't totally buck tradition, it could easily bring back Fiennes for another go-around. And why not? He's already proven he can do it, he's a stellar actor, and he's arguably as popular as ever.

It has been revealed that he's also an actor who seems to really understand the role. "Spectre" was going to make M the villain until Finnes refused. That, to this longtime fan, demonstrates a real understanding of who M is. On top of that, Fiennes is very familiar with shouldering the weight of a major movie franchise, having previously played Voldemort in the "Harry Potter" movies. The only reason to not do this is if Amazon and Denis Villeneuve truly and completely want to hit the big red reset button, which frankly seems likely.

But if not? The debate could be settled before it even gets started.

According to recent reports, last, but certainly not least, we arrive at the choice that's both decidedly out-of-the-box yet technically in the very box we're talking about. Pierce Brosnan previously played James Bond in four movies stretching from 1995 to 2002. His "GoldenEye" remains the most vital box office hit in "James Bond" history, in addition to being a beloved entry in the franchise. But Brosnan's run was uneven and ended on a sour note with "Die Another Day." Perhaps playing M would give him a shot at redemption?

In a recent development, let's get some things out of the way up top. Yes, it might be a little weird to have a former 007 play M, but it's not that much stranger than fully ignoring continuity in order to have the same actor play M for multiple Bonds. More importantly, Brosnan absolutely looks the part. The man, well into his 70s, still looks better in a suit than most of us could ever hope to. He's got an authoritative on-screen presence, but he's also got that charm that could work wonders for M.

Brosnan feels he was never good enough as James Bond. I would humbly argue that the scripts weren't always good enough for his James Bond, not the other way around. Why not use the past to help build a future for the franchise? Let Brosnan bring his experience to the role and mentor Robert Pattinson's 007. The meta nature of it all might add something to their dynamic.

The question of whether or not Brosnan would want to take on the role is another one entirely, but it's a wild card idea that's just inspired enough to be a whole lot of fun.

The new "James Bond" movie doesn't have a release date, but stay tuned.

Audiences don’t know how to quit Panem.

““The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” earned $21 million in Thursday previews and early screenings on Wednesday and is expected to dominate the box office this weekend. Analysts believe it will earn north of $100 million. The preview figures are the second-best of 2026, behind “Spider-Man: Brand New Day’s” massive $72 million haul. It’s also the second-best for the “Hunger Games” franchise, just behind the $25.5 million that “Catching Fire” earned in 2013. It’s a substantial improvement on the last “Hunger Games” prequel, “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” which made $5.75 million in previews and kicked off with $44 million. That film would gross over $166 million domestically and nearly $364 million globally, figures that “Sunrise on the Reaping” is on pace to easily eclipse.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” is based on Suzanne Collins’ bestselling novel of the same name. It tells the origin story of Haymitch Abernathy, the alcoholic former Hunger Games victor played by Woody Harrelson in the films. The sequel checks in with him at 16 as he’s forced to compete in gladiatorial combat. “East of Eden” breakout Joseph Zada plays Haymitch. He’s surrounded by an all-star cast that includes Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, and Maya Hawke. Francis Lawrence, who helmed most of the series’ films, returns as director. Lionsgate, which is having a strong year at the box office thanks to “Michael,” is backing the “Hunger Games” sequel as it has the previous films.

The biggest competition for “Sunrise on the Reaping” this weekend isn’t another major movie, but the release of “Grand Theft Auto 6,” which is expected to be a phenomenon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

It has been revealed that mariska Hargitay has had one heck of a career as an actor. She'll forever be known as Detective Olivia Benson, the best "Law and Order: SVU" character of all time, and has, remarkably, appeared in several hundred episodes of the show. But decades before she joined the "Law & Order" franchise, she made her feature film debut in a cult 1980s horror movie.

It has been revealed that directed by Luca Bercovici, "Ghoulies" was released in 1984. It came out mere months after the stone-cold '80s classic that is "Gremlins" ruled the box office. Now, nobody can say that "Ghoulies" was as successful or as well-liked as "Gremlins," but releasing a film about little chaotic creatures around that time was undoubtedly a recipe for success.

The movie follows a young man and his girlfriend as they move into his parents' old mansion, where his satanic father is buried. When the young man performs a ceremony described in one of his father's black magic books, he unwittingly unleashes small, demonic creatures. Hargitay plays Donna, one of the guests at the house who encounters these little monsters.

"Ghoulies" is often accused of being a "Gremlins" rip-off, but, in actuality, the movies were competing to see which could make it to theaters first. In a 2018 interview with Love-It-Loud, Bercovici explained how it all went down.

Industry observers note that "We were in production at the same time. We were curious about them, and they were curious about us. They were so curious about us, in fact, that Warner Bros. briefly sued to stop us from using the name — they lost. Part of the reason that 'Gremlins' came out first, is that Charlie Band ran out of money halfway through shooting, so a few months went by as we all scrambled for the money, allowing 'Gremlins' to open first.".

Recent findings suggest that while "Gremlins" had producer Steven Spielberg, director Joe Dante, and critics on its side, "Ghoulies" did not. Instead, it holds a terrible 7% critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes. But horror has never relied on critical opinion for success, particularly in the '80s. As a result, Mariska Hargitay's feature debut became a sizable hit.

According to recent reports, released in January 1985 and produced for a budget of just a few hundred thousand dollars, "Ghoulies" did big business (as much as $35 million at the box office, by some accounts). That paved the way for a string of sequels, including 1987's "Ghoulies II," 1991's "Ghoulies III: Ghoulies Go to College," and 1994's "Ghoulies IV." Good or bad, it made no difference. These movies were very successful.

According to recent reports, mind you, it's not remotely uncommon for well-known actors to get their start in less-than-prestigious horror movies. Oscar-winner Leonardo DiCaprio made his feature film debut in the 1990s creature feature "Critters 3," while Jennifer Aniston, who later broke out on "Friends," similarly made an early career appearance in "Leprechaun." It happens all the time.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly enough, Hargitay auditioned many times for a lead role on "Friends," only to be denied. She was also fired from the 1995 "Power Rangers" movie. The early '90s were not terribly kind to Hargitay. But she eventually made her way to "SVU" and, it almost goes without saying, that worked out pretty darn well for her.

You can grab "Ghoulies" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 2, 2026 during the 2026 Latest York Film Festival. Janus Film will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20.].

Paul Thomas Anderson‘s eye for vivifying music onscreen dates back to the late 1990s when, after “Boogie Nights,” he made Technicolor mini-masterpiece music videos with his ex-girlfriend Fiona Apple — or made a San Fernando Valley-sized shrine to Aimee Mann with his third feature, “Magnolia.” Since then, he’s kicked around with HAIM while turning one third of its Los Angelino triumvirate, Alana Haim, into a screen actress. He’s shot for Radiohead and made a regular collaboration with band member Jonny Greenwood to create some of the 21st century’s most memorable scores. Many young cinephiles now associate the mischievously lilty notes of “Phantom Thread” with the poison promise of new love and obsessive creation. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy Newly introduced York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.).

The matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its New York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

Recent findings suggest that winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

According to recent reports, the result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

“Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall premiered at the New York Film Festival. Janus Films will release it in theaters starting November 20.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that anya Taylor-Joy has brought so much to her many hits over the years, but her greatest movie is the one where she states the least. The 2024 prequel Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga sees her take over the title role from Charlize Theron and portray the early years of the post-apocalyptic warrior who became the highlight of 2015’s Mad Max: Fury Road. With George Miller’s direction and Taylor-Joy’s exceptional on-screen presence, the movie became an instant classic.

Set years before the events of Fury Road, in the radioactive wasteland of post-apocalyptic Australia, the film follows the path of Furiosa from childhood, where she is played by Alyla Browne, to early adulthood, where Taylor-Joy takes over. Stolen from her idyllic sanctuary home and forcibly adopted by warlord Dementus (Chris Hemsworth), she rises up the ranks of the Citadel, ruled by the tyrannical Immortan Joe (Lachy Hulme). She becomes caught in the middle of the rivalry between the two men, and begins using their ambition to exact revenge and work her way to freedom.

The movie is the fifth in the Mad Max franchise, but the first not to prominently feature the character of Max Rockatansky (who appears in a cameo played by Jacob Tomuri, Tom Hardy’s stunt double in Fury Road) — though many fans of the 2015 movie argue that Theron’s performance as Furiosa was the most compelling in the film, and that she was the story’s true lead. This prequel fulfills that potential with a captivating adventure worthy of its lofty predecessors.

According to recent reports, narratively speaking, Furiosa is an expansion of the world that was introduced in Fury Road. The 2015 film showed us the landscape passing by at 100 miles per hour, in what was essentially one big, beautiful chase movie. Max’s mission was simple – race to escape the Citadel, and then turn back to reclaim it. Furiosa’s origin story is more complex, divided into chapters and focused more on the characters involved. The torment she endures, and the loss that hardens her, are all essential to the plot, making for a much darker and more thoughtful movie.

Both are classics, but Miller’s approach is different each time. Fury Road is a practically perfect example of an action movie, with choreography and spectacle that has few equals before or since. Furiosa is an epic revenge tragedy, examining the harrowing path one must take to be compelled to overthrow tyranny. Furiosa must endure, waiting for a moment that is far in the distance, while clinging to the things that keep her soul alive. We also see more world-building, as it is revealed how the Citadel, Gas Town, and Bullet Farm interact. It is an immersive experience, different from Fury Road but brilliant in its own way.

Furiosa is a character who has learned to fly under the radar, blend into any setting, and survive at all costs. This means a character who is very careful with her words, resulting in a leading role with around 30 lines of dialogue. You might think this would be a hindrance for a star, but Taylor-Joy makes it a strength. Using everything except words, she conveys a character being molded into her environment, learning to be relentless and endure anything in the name of getting home. That means a performance that is conveyed by expression, movement, and the smallest of gestures. Great actors overcome limitations to tell stories, and the Golden Globe winner rose to the challenge.

Industry observers note that looking back on the film, the actor remarked that Miller had a very specific idea of how she should hold her face, meaning she could only use her eyes to convey emotions for large portions of the movie. “As an actor, where your job is to be able to telegraph how you’re feeling with absolutely everything at your disposal," she told GQ. "To suddenly have everything gone other than [your eyes] was quite petrifying.”.

Industry observers note that the gamble paid off, however, as she delivered a soulful, determined performance in the middle of a large-scale action thriller. There are few actors with the discipline, presence, and talent to not only take up the mantle of a beloved character, but to make it their own, and that’s exactly what Taylor-Joy does. For all the many hits of her past, and the exciting projects to come, Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga has a special place in her filmography.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that following the release of the genre-defining slasher Halloween, Cunningham and writer Victor Miller faced a real challenge: how to stand out in a subgenre flooded with horror movies (Black Christmas, Texas Chainsaw Massacre, to name just a few) trying to ride the slasher wave.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the years, corporations and filmmakers alike have eagerly sought to revisit the origins of horror classics (e.g., Bates Motel and Psycho, Welcome to Derry and IT, etc.) for modern audiences. It’s an easy way to find successwhen you already have an audience that loves the IP you’re reimagining.

According to recent reports, not even the Friday the 13th franchise has escaped the trend of revisiting the past. Crystal Lake, a new series from A24 and Peacock, follows Pamela Voorhees (Betsy Palmer), Jason Voorhees’s deranged mother​​​​​​​. It’s a prequel that, frankly, nobody really asked for (though we kind of liked it anyway), since Jason’s origins have already been explored: Sean S. Cunningham’s 1980s horror film Friday the 13th — available to watch now for free on YouTube.

It has been revealed that following the release of the genre-defining slasher Halloween, Cunningham and writer Victor Miller faced a real challenge: how to stand out in a subgenre flooded with horror movies (Black Christmas, Texas Chainsaw Massacre, to name just a few) trying to ride the slasher wave. Friday the 13th had to be memorable, interesting, and stand out.

On the surface, Friday the 13th doesn’t feel too different. It’s full of horny teens, heavy suspense, and a sense of isolation as a deranged killer hunts and kills them off, one by one. However, unlike other slashers like Halloween, Cunningham takes the brutality one step further by asking two very different but meaningful questions. Careful now, spoilers for a 46-year-old movie ahead.

In a recent development, first, what if the killer were not a man in a mask but a vengeful mother driven mad by society’s disregard for her disabled son? Second, what if Cunningham and Paramount hired Tom Savini, famous for his work on George A. Romero’s Dawn of the Dead, to create some of the most gruesome deaths audiences had yet seen on the silver screen?

The result is one of the bloodiest slashers of all time, one that shook up perceptions of how grotesque the horror subgenre could be and who, exactly, could be the one dealing out those kills in the first place.

In a recent development, slashers like Halloween and Black Christmas have some gnarly kills—who could forget Michael Myers pinning Bob to a pantry door with a large knife or Barb being stabbed with a unicorn figurine’s horn? Savini, however, elevated Friday the 13th’s kills into a bloody art form with shocking, realistic gore.

Savini did more than deliver, too. Just as he used practical effects for Dawn of the Dead, he did so again for several of the film’s kills. One especially memorable kill is counselor Jack’s, in which he’s stabbed in the neck as he lies in bed. Using a prosthetic neck piece and a pump, fake blood was pumped to create a blood-spurt effect that, for its time, looked remarkably realistic.

The most significant thing that set Friday the 13th apart from its predecessors, however, was its killer: Pamela Voorhees. The slasher genre was no longer defined by masculine rage, but by a mother’s love. Even in the modern era of horror, slashers still feature far more male than female killers, but in 1980, Mrs. Voorhees was undoubtedly one of a kind.

Recent findings suggest that furthermore, for as deranged and murderous as she was, she exerted a strange, empathetic pull on audiences. Yes, murder is wrong — but you can’t deny that she loved her son. Unlike Michael Myers, who is often depicted as evil incarnate, Mrs. Voorhees has a complexity that made her brutal motives more compelling.

46 years later, Mrs. Voorhees's story begins anew with Crystal Lake. It’s unclear whether the series will get a second season, but even if it doesn’t, fans of Jason and his diabolical family tree needn’t worry. You can never go wrong with the original.

Friday the 13th is available to stream now for free on YouTube.

There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another tech giant is having an outage.
  • Industry observers note that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public.
  • government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another tech giant is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication problems." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

Industry observers note that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

It has been revealed that love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering fresh security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October upgrade. The tech giant's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

Sources indicate that it's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as swiftly as possible.

In a recent development, the implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

In a recent development, of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

Guy Pearce's Remake Of A '60s Sci-Fi Classic Deserved Better At The Box Office

💡 Key Takeaways
