  • Recent findings suggest that the movie isn't great, reducing the intellectualism of Wells' original novel into a rote sci-fi action thriller, but there was a steampunk quirkiness to "The Time Machine" that could have been more openly embraced.
  • Guy Pearce plays Alexander Hartdegen, the inventor of the titular device, and he learns very quickly that mucking around with time travel doesn't always provide the result he's after.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that simon Wells' 2002 sci-fi flick "The Time Machine" was extrapolated from H.G. Wells' celebrated 1895 novel, one of the best sci-fi novels ever written, and also from George Pal's famed 1960 adaptation of the same story, itself one of the best time travel movies of all time. Made for a budget of $80 million, "The Time Machine" didn't overwhelm at the box office, earning almost $124 million worldwide. Critics were very unkind to "The Time Machine," and the film only has a 28% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 151 reviews.

Recent findings suggest that the movie isn't great, reducing the intellectualism of Wells' original novel into a rote sci-fi action thriller, but there was a steampunk quirkiness to "The Time Machine" that could have been more openly embraced. It was even nominated for an Oscar for Best Makeup.

Guy Pearce plays Alexander Hartdegen, the inventor of the titular device, and he learns very quickly that mucking around with time travel doesn't always provide the result he's after. Alexander's motivation for building a time machine in the first place is to go back in time to prevent the murder of his fiancée (Sienna Guillory). This isn't part of the original novel, nor of George Pal's movie. Alexander spends five years building the time machine, and manages to save his fiancée, only to lose her again shortly thereafter. Something about the universe requires she die.

This kicks off a long-ranging time-travel adventure wherein Alexander begins tripping through the centuries, hoping to find an answer about how fate operates. He eventually ends up in the very, very distant future — specifically, the year AD 802,701 — when humanity has evolved into two distinct subspecies, the Morlocks and the Eloi.

The two most notable additions to the movie of "The Time Machine" that most dramatically depart from the previous versions are characters played by Orlando Jones and Jeremy Irons. Jones' character is, I would argue, a good addition, adding someone for the protagonist to converse with. Irons' character is ... well, his inclusion is just baffling.

According to recent reports, jones plays Vox 114, an artificially intelligent digital library aide from the year 2030 who appears on glass screens. Because he is a computer, Vox is eager to teach people about science and the world. When Alexander, having just jaunted forward in time, asks Vox about time travel, Vox gets a little impatient, thinking Alexander just wants to talk about science fiction. Later in the film, Alexander finds Vox in a cave, somehow still operational hundreds of centuries later. Vox seems to have developed something of a consciousness over the years. He also still has a complete memory, remembering Alexander from this sojourn to 2030.

In a recent development, irons, meanwhile, plays a character credited as the Über-Morlock, the psychic Cenobite-like leader of the Morlocks. As anyone who has read H.G. Wells' book can tell you, the Morlocks were an underground race of ape-like beings who feed on the Eloi who live on the Earth's surface. The Eloi, meanwhile, are placid, gentle, and defenseless. The idea is that the Morlocks evolved from old Earth's laboring classes, and the Eloi evolved from its aristocracy. Wells was clearly making a comment on class divisions, and how they will eventually play out if left to evolve along their logical extremes.

There is no Über-Morlock leading the underground monsters in the original book, and the inclusion of such a character in the 2002 movie is confusing and strange.

Industry observers note that that mentioned, there is at least something delicious about Jeremy Irons' performance. He sports a long white wig, pasty white skin, and wears a bizarre, black pleather outfit that looks like it could be worn to a bondage bar. "The Time Machine" climaxes with the Über-Morlock and Alexander grappling while the machine hurtles forward in time millions of years. It's such a kooky conceit that you might find yourself enjoying "The Time Machine.".

Recent findings suggest that some fun trivia: Simon Wells, the director of "The Time Machine" just happens to be the great-grandson of H.G. Wells. Simon Wells also co-directed the 1991 animated film "An American Tail: Fievel Goes West" (which was Jimmy Stewart's final film), as well as "We're Back! A Dinosaur's Story," the giant '90s animated hit "The Prince of Egypt," and several others. (He also helmed the massive Disney flop "Mars Needs Moms," but we'll forgive him this time.) All of this is to say that Wells was no neophyte in 2002, and he is not a traditional nepo baby who received an opportunity primarily because of his lineage.

Recent findings suggest that critics largely hated "The Time Machine." Roger Ebert gave the film one-and-a-half stars out of four, saying that it was "a witless recycling of the H.G. Wells story from 1895, with the absurdity intact but the wonderment missing." He noted that 800,000 years into the future, it was awfully convenient that Morlock and Eloi both seem to speak English. Guy Pearce's performance also didn't match the material. Ebert wrote that "Pearce, as the hero, makes the mistake of trying to give a good and realistic performance. Irons at least knows what kind of movie he's in, and hams it up accordingly.".

Okay, so "The Time Machine" is not great. But Irons is fun. It certainly didn't deserve to bomb.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

According to recent reports, to aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole upcoming task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

“Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a new idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”.

To that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try new looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro said. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”.

Industry observers note that hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro remarked the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

In a recent development, “I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro said. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

Industry observers note that hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The important part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro said, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I quickly made a latest design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”.

Sources indicate that in addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro mentioned. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”.

During one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and said, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

Industry observers note that “He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro remarked. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The legacy-quel is alive and well, and it only makes sense that a sequel/reboot/reimagining would eventually come for “Home Alone,” Chris Columbus’ 1990 holiday classic starring Macaulay Culkin.

There was buzz that Culkin over the summer pitched an idea to Disney as to where a grown Kevin McAllister would be today after enduring two child abandonments and harassment and attempted murder from bumbling bandits (our interpretation, not necessarily his read on Kevin’s childhood shenanigans and trauma). Disney now seems to have warmed to the idea like a cup of hot cocoa, especially thanks to the two additional names who are working with Culkin on the project: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.

Things are very, very early days, and any plot details are being kept under wraps for now, and no director is attached at the moment.

Chris Columbus directed the original “Home Alone” and its nearly-as-loved sequel “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York,” and both written by the late great John Hughes. If you can believe it, there have been six “Home Alone” movies in all, with the third one at least released in theaters and doing respectable box office numbers. The others are all TV movies or in the case of the most recent 2021 film “Home Sweet Home Alone,” a Disney+ streaming movie.

In a recent development, the original two films though grossed $477 million and $358 million worldwide, respectively, and the original still gets tons of cable play and finds its way into the Nielsen streaming charts. It makes sense that a more serious sequel with Culkin back in the fold would be welcomed by audiences.

Sadly, “Home Alone” has been back on the minds of audiences of late after the recent passing of Catherine O’Hara, who played Kevin’s mom, and also Tim Curry, who had a small role as a hotel clerk in “Home Alone 2.” Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern as the Wet Bandits are still around, though Pesci has been mostly retired outside of his return in Scorsese’s “The Irishman” back in 2019 and his role in the Pete Davidson Peacock series “Bupkis” in 2023.

Culkin too has had a bit of a resurgence, making a cameo in the most recent season of “Fallout” and doing a voice in Disney’s “Zootopia 2.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ben Brewster is a filmmaker, critic, screenwriter, and actor whose work sits at the intersection of film culture, craft analysis, and storytelling.

He is a movie list contributing writer at Collider and a contributing writer for High on Films, where he covers contemporary cinema, independent film, and festival releases with an eye toward narrative structure, performance, and visual language.

Ben is an active film festival participant, having worked with Newport Film, the Nantucket Film Festival and as a screener for the Austin, Boston & Woodstock film festivals. He brings to that work a programming instinct shaped by years of close engagement with independent and documentary cinema. This comes with a deep investment in the kinds of films that rarely find their way into the mainstream conversation without someone willing to advocate for them.

Recent findings suggest that his background spans documentary and narrative filmmaking, film marketing, and production, including work with award-winning directors. This as well as developing his own indie production company, Lilac Creative Studio, through which he develops and produces original work across fiction and nonfiction forms. His debut documentary, Diamond in the Rust, is an examination of economic redevelopment and displacement in the Queens area of New York City. The film was recently accepted to the Unisphere Film Festival, the Defense of Democracy Film Festival, and the Urbanite Arts & Film Festival. This would mark his first festival recognition as a director. In addition to his writing and programming work, Ben hosts Beneath the Bloom, a film podcast exploring the work behind the scenes in cinema, and the struggles one can face to make a movie become a reality. The show reflects the same sensibility that runs through all of his work. A conviction that film is not merely entertainment but one of the most powerful tools human beings have for understanding each other.

Across mediums, his work is driven by a deep belief in film as a communal, transformative art form.

In a recent development, in the 2010s, war films felt odd and hard to pin down. The fighting in Iraq and Afghanistan was still running its course. At the same time, World War II veterans were passing away one by one. Hollywood looked two ways in response. It nodded back to the older "good war" stories that shaped the genre for years. It also faced newer conflicts that did not end neatly. No clear heroes always showed up. Because of that, many movies seemed to argue with each other about what a war film is supposed to do and what it is supposed to stand for in this decade.

The top films from that era share one main trait: intensity. This was the period of films that try to place you right in the middle of events. Directors like Christopher Nolan and Sam Mendes leaned into big, crisp images and shots that do not cut away for a long time. The goal was simple, even if the work was not. Put the viewer in the mud and the water. Other filmmakers, including Kathryn Bigelow and Peter Berg, leaned toward a documentary kind of drive. Their stories often felt like they came straight from headlines. Even the sound mattered a lot. In several cases, major awards recognized the way these films made gunshots, machinery and quiet hit hard in the gut.

Some movies in this list got mixed reviews from critics. A few of the highest earners also stirred strong reactions. This happened most often when the films dealt with tense recent history. If you sort them by Rotten Tomatoes scores, you get a quick, not necessarily wholistic view of what some critics thought at the time. That method is by no means perfect. Scores do not always say how a film has held up later. They also do not always match what viewers liked. The range here is wide. There are grim POW survival stories. There are also very detailed retellings of real military missions, scene by scene. These are the most intense war films of the decade, ranked.

It has been revealed that angelina Jolie directed Unbroken, based on Laura Hillenbrand's 2010 book about Olympic runner and bombardier Louis Zamperini. The film stars Jack O'Connell as Zamperini, who survives a plane crash in the Pacific. He drifts on a raft for 47 days before being captured and taken away by the Japanese. O'Connell plays him with a wiry, stubborn energy, with Jolie cutting between flashbacks to his boyhood and his running days in between the horrors. He lands in prison camps under the cruel corporal Watanabe (Miyavi), known as the Bird, who runs the prison camp. The great Roger Deakins captured the open ocean and shot the muddy camps in wide, painterly-like frames.

Sources indicate that joel and Ethan Coen, Richard LaGravenese, and William Nicholson share the screenplay credit. Unbroken opened on Christmas Day 2014 and grossed $163 million worldwide. Rotten Tomatoes lists Unbroken at 52%, and its consensus calls it well-intentioned but too dependent on overly familiar prestige war genre beats. Deakins earned an Oscar nomination for his cinematography, and the National Board of Review named the film one of its top ten of the year, despite the Oscar bait it had written all over it. Many felt the story became a long parade of suffering, although the audience score was friendly, landing at 70%. Zamperini died in July 2014, a few months before it opened, and a faith-based sequel, Unbroken: Path to Redemption, followed in 2018.

Clint Eastwood directed American Sniper at age 84. It is a biopic of Navy SEAL Chris Kyle, the most lethal sniper in U.S. military history. He's a Texas cowboy who netted the nickname Legend for his pinpoint accuracy in Iraq. Bradley Cooper bulked up for the role, and plays Kyle across four tours in Iraq, as he struggles to connect with his wife at home, Taya (Siena Miller). Jason Hall adapted the script directly from Kyle's memoir, with the film cutting from Iraqi rooftops to quiet kitchen scenes in Texas. Rotten Tomatoes lists it at 71% from critics and 84% from audiences, and moviegoers gave it an A+ CinemaScore.

The opening scene, in which Kyle must decide whether to fire at a child carrying a grenade, sets a tense tone. A rival sniper known as Mustafa gives the story a cat and mouse thread. Cooper earned a Best Actor nomination, one of six Oscar nominations that included Best Picture and a win for Sound Editing. American Sniper grossed $547.6 million worldwide on a $58 million budget, marking it as Eastwood's highest grossing film, and the biggest January release ever up to that point. Controversy followed, with critics arguing about its heroic portrait of Kyle and its historical liberties. More than a decade later, it landed in Netflix's top 10 with 4.4 million views in a single week.

Recent findings suggest that david Ayer wrote and directed Fury, which follows a five-man Sherman tank crew pushing through Germany in April 1945. It's when the war's last days are its most brutal, and Brad Pitt plays Wardaddy, a battle-scarred sergeant who has kept his crew alive since North Africa. Logan Lerman is Norman Ellison, a young typist forced into the crew, with Shia LaBeouf, Michael Peña, and Jon Bernthal as the veterans who both mock and protect him. Ayer allegedly put the cast through a brutal boot camp before filming.

Sources indicate that fury grossed $211.8 million and opened at No.1 at the box office on a budget of about $68 million. The production used a real Tiger tank, Tiger 131, the only operational Tiger in the world. Rotten Tomatoes lists it at 75% from critics, and 84% from audiences. The consensus calls it a well acted, raw depiction of war that does not fully live up to its lofty ambitions. James Berardinelli praised how it reveals the horrors of war without reveling in cruelty, while LA Weekly's Amy Nicholson felt that Ayer wallowed in ugliness. Ayer drew on the real 2nd Armored Division, nicknamed Hell on Wheels.

Recent findings suggest that 1917 follows two young British soldiers on a single day in April 1917, and Sam Mendes built it to look like one unbroken shot. George MacKay and Dean-Charles Chapman play Lance Corporals Schofield and Blake, two young British soldiers sent across no man's land to deliver a message that could save 1,600 men from a German trap. Mendes co-wrote the story with Krysty Wilson-Cairns, drawing on tales his grandfather Alfred Mendes told him about WWI.

Sources indicate that roger Deakins shot through trenches, craters, and rivers, and captured a burning town without a visible cut. Colin Firth, Benedict Cumberbatch, Mark Strong, and Andrew Scott appear in brief but memorable roles. Rotten Tomatoes lists 1917 at 88% from 472 reviews, and its consensus calls it hard-hitting, immersive and an impressive technical achievement. The movie won three Oscars, garnering a Best Picture nomination as well. It also took home the BAFTA for Best Film and the Golden Globes for Best Motion Picture, Drama and Best Director. The night sequence in a burning town lit by flares and the final run across the battlefield are the most visually stunning sequences.

In a recent development, zero Dark Thirty opens with darkness and the sound of real 9/11 calls. Kathryn Bigelow directed the film off a script from Mark Boal, her collaborator on The Hurt Locker. Bigelow constantly stresses the stakes, with Jessica Chastain as the lead Maya, a CIA analyst whose obsession has driven a decade's worth of work hunting Osama bin Laden. The film then pivots to harsh and brutal interrogation scenes, with Jason Clarke playing the interrogator Dan, and Jennifer Ehle, Kyle Chandler, Mark Strong, and Joel Edgerton rounding out the cast.

Recent findings suggest that rotten Tomatoes lists it at 91% from 304 reviews, with an 80% audience score. Boal's script moves like a procedural, with offices, briefings, and dead ends. Critics called it gripping, suspenseful, and brilliantly crafted. Chastain earned an Oscar nomination for Best Actress, and the movie tied with Skyfall for Best Sound Editing. The final 30 minutes recreate the May 2011 raid on the Abbottabad compound in dim green night vision, and the sequence is considered among the most tense in modern war movies. Controversy surrounding its torture scenes has never faded, and some critics now see the movie differently after the 2014 torture report.

Dunkirk divides its story into three timelines, one week on the beach, one day at sea, and one hour in the air. Christopher Nolan depicts the 1940 evacuation of Allied troops through the perspective of Tommy (Fionn Whitehead), a young solider hunting for any way off the sand, and Harrier (Tom Hardy), a spitfire pilot with a failing fuel gauge. Mark Rylance is a man named Mr. Dawson, a civilian who sails his boat across the channel to help rescue troops. Kenneth Branagh, Cillian Murphy, Harry Styles, Barry Keoghan and Jack Lowden appear in the ensemble. Hoyte van Hoytema shot it in large format, and Hans Zimmer's score keeps a ticking clock running in the background.

Sources indicate that rotten Tomatoes lists Dunkirk at 92%, with an 81% audience score. Nolan used real ships and planes which gave the beaches and skies a physical weight. The consensus describes the project as an emotionally satisfying spectacle from a writer-director in full command of his craft. Dunkirk grossed more than $500 million worldwide and saw eight Oscar nominations, including Best Picture and Best Director. Between the grand practical effects, the dialogue is sparse, and the sound design carries much of the tension. Critics have called it one of the most immersive war movies ever and one of the best movies of the 2010s.

Sources indicate that prequel film "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" reveals the details of how Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada, Woody Harrelson in the original films) won the 50th Hunger Games ... and lost everything else in his life, turning him into a miserable man using alcohol to cope. Yet "The Hunger Games: Catching Fire" revealed Haymitch wasn't merely the burnout he first appeared to be, but a key member of the rebellion against the Capitol.

Beetee and Haymitch collaborate as part of a conspiracy to have Haymitch disrupt the arena's mechanical systems and, hopefully, sabotage the Games once he's inside. When Haymitch does so, but the Games persist and, when the conspiracy is discovered, he takes the fall. The Capitol has already done the worst thing it could to Beetee by taking his son, and as a victor, he's too valuable and visible a symbol to kill.

It has been revealed that "Hunger Games" fans already know this isn't the last we've seen of Beetee, and this probably isn't the first you've seen of his actor who plays him. Born in Upcoming Orleans in 1994, Harrison is the son of two musicians, but he chose acting as his primary creative path.

Harrison's film career began with incidental parts in "12 Years A Slave" and "Ender's Game" in 2013, which were followed by his first starring role in 2017's post-apocalyptic horror film "It Comes At Night." Sources indicate that in 2018, Harrison appeared in "Monster," Netflix's adaptation of Walter Dean Myers's 1999 novel about a Black honor student accused of murder. Luce is a straight-A student, popular athlete, and seemingly on his way to great things ... until he writes an essay that appears to defend radical political violence as a valid means of change.

According to recent reports, having proved himself with those leading roles, Harrison has continued making himself into one of Hollywood's most prolific young actors even before joining "The Hunger Games." King. Harrison also played Martin Luther King Jr. in Season 4 of National Geographic series "Genius," opposite Aaron Pierre (now known as John Stewart from "Lanterns") as Malcolm X.

Industry observers note that but that's not all Harrison can do. He played Christian de Neuvillette in Joe Wright's 2021 musical film "Cyrano," adapting the 1897 French play by Edmond Rostand. In 2024 "Lion King" prequel "Mufasa," he voiced Scar. Being in tech giant with Jeremy Irons and Chiwetel Ejiofor is pretty impressive for an actor Harrison's age.

In a recent development, for over 30 years, Bosch has been a standout thriller series, and the author, Michael Connelly, hasn't stopped surprising readers. In his fresh release, Connelly delves further into the background and origin of the protagonist, Harry Bosch, than ever, shedding new light on his development.

It has been revealed that when audiences first met Bosch in the 1992 novel, The Black Echo, Connelly introduced us to the world of the LAPD homicide detective and the cases he solves. Of course, things promptly get personal for Bosch as his background as a soldier in the Vietnam War and troubled past influence how he solves some grisly murders in Los Angeles. The Bosch TV show has done an amazing job bringing Connelly's novels to life, but it's always exciting when the writer adds texture to his backstory in the novels.

Industry observers note that the most recent Bosch book, The Hollow, was released this past year in October 2026, and is the 26th volume in the Bosch franchise. Though Harry Bosch has come a long way since his early days solving crimes for the LAPD, Connelly keeps raising the bar, finding newly introduced ways to expand his story and crafting unbelievable thrillers that readers can't put down. Currently rated at 4.48 stars on Goodreads, The Hollow debuted to a warm reception because it takes us back to the beginning of Bosch's history.

Of course, readers know that Harry Bosch hasn't always had the easiest life, and Connelly has explored his past before, but The Hollow goes further than ever before, digging into Bosch's childhood. Just because Bosch retired from the LAPD, his time stopping criminals is far from over, and in the 2026 book, it's more emotional than ever. The Hollow touches upon Bosch's experience as a ward of the state as a child in the wake of his mother's murder.

Recent findings suggest that his half-brother, Mickey Haller, tells Bosch that MacLaren Children’s Center, where Bosch suffered abuse as a child, has finally been busted in a class-action lawsuit, and Bosch is entitled to a huge settlement. However, money isn't what interests Bosch. Though he's tried to hide from this dark period of his past for a long time, Bosch is determined to solve the long-cold case of a child, Chops, he knew at MacLaren, who was found dead.

With his investigative skills and the fact that he can no longer pretend that Chops' death doesn't haunt him, Bosch has all the fuel he needs to track down the predator whom he believes killed Chops. The central villain in The Hollow is a shocking antagonist, making Bosch's investigation all the more compelling as he closes in on him. However, the most arresting part of The Hollow isn't the case, but Bosch's arc coming to grips with the abuse he faced as a child.

In a recent development, the Hollow is an emotional, intense book and one of Connelly's most cathartic, as the novel pulls no punches when it comes to bringing Bosch face to face with some of the most traumatic moments of his childhood. The Bosch franchise has always touched upon heavy themes, as Connelly's thriller novels explore dark criminal cases and murders. However, the personal element of The Hollow, and the way Bosch grows as a character throughout the story, make it a worthy addition to Connelly's work.

It makes sense that reviews of The Hollow have been positive, as it satisfies longtime fans who were hoping to get deeper insight into Bosch and his background. Though it's not the best place to start when beginning the Bosch novels, The Hollow was a vital addition to the canon and will be remembered as a pivotal volume that changed the way we see Harry Bosch forever.

How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing.
  • Industry observers note that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire.
  • Recent findings suggest that the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be notable for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Industry observers note that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”.

Recent findings suggest that the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be notable for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

It has been revealed that “When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was important to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado said. “.

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

For Crawford, the major lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

It has been revealed that “The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”.

Still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

Recent findings suggest that “Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado said. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”.

Sources indicate that this all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford said, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other big studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

Curry Barker Would Have Completely Reshot ‘Obsession’ If He Could

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker.
  • Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.
  • In a recent development, “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really quickly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” remarked Barker on Toolkit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-announced third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a Fresh Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles.

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

In a recent development, “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really quickly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” remarked Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”.

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

In a recent development, “It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” mentioned Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”.

Sources indicate that barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” said Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”.

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”.

Industry observers note that “People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” remarked Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”.

One of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how promptly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

In a recent development, “I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” mentioned Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”.

Directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

What Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, quickly says he fell short in “Obsession.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” said Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”.

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

According to recent reports, “Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” stated Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”.

As Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

It has been revealed that “I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”.

“I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you're the kind of person who has fun spotting celebrities in roles they took before they were launched to the heights of their fame, you could do a lot worse than throwing on a few episodes of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and keeping your eye out for guest stars. Before he starred in "The Rocketeer" and took on the infamous Transylvanian count in "Bram Stoker's Dracula," Billy Campbell played the roguish Okona in "TNG's" second season, and before she had her breakout role in "Double Jeopardy" opposite Tommy Lee Jones, Ashley Judd made her acting debut in Season 5, playing an ensign in the episode where the crew of the Enterprise were all taken over by an evil video game.

These early appearances are always fun to catch, especially when the actor you're spotting is both immediately recognizable and just about to break out heights so high that you'd almost need a starship to catch up to them. The best example? Kirsten Dunst, who made an appearance in the final season of "The Next Generation," long before she'd star as Mary Jane Watson in Sam Raimi's "Spider-Man" films.

On the Season 7 episode "Dark Page", an 11-year-old Dunst played Hedril, a member of the Cairn, a species of alien telepaths who, as Captain Picard puts it, "have no concept of spoken language." To help facilitate communication, the Federation sends in their own telepath, occasional ambassador and perpetual thorn in Picard's side Lwaxana Troi (Majel Barrett), the mother of the Enterprise's empathic counselor Deanna Troi (Marina Sirtis).

Unfortunately, the Cairn's first attempt at connecting with an alien species goes awry, and Hedril winds up triggering Lwaxana's repressed memories of Deanna's older sister Kestra, who died when Deanna was a baby.

As a result, Dunst plays both Hedril and, in scenes where Deanna has to explore her mom's mindscape to find out while she's in a coma, a version of Kestra — who, it should be noted, had never been seen or mentioned before on the series, and was even unknown to Deanna.

It has been revealed that the episode aired in 1993, and while it wasn't Dunst's first role as a child actress, it was the most prominent by far at the time. Of course, that would all change the following year with the release of "Interview With the Vampire," in which Dunst had her true breakout role playing the vampire Claudia, alongside Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt. Despite Pitt's difficulties in filming that led him to start feeling like an actual vampire, the movie was a financial and critical success, and Dunst in particular earned praise from Roger Ebert for the role and an MTV Movie Award for Best Supporting Actress and a Golden Globe nomination.

Dunst would go on to bigger fame as the star of the iconic cheerleading comedy "Bring It On" and, of course, the romantic lead of Sam Raimi's "Spider-Man" trilogy. As for Hedril, she was one of many one-off characters who never returned to the Enterprise, but Kestra had a bit more of an interesting legacy. A novel set in an alternate universe called "Q and A" cast her, and not Deanna, as the counselor of the Enterprise, and in the first season of "Star Trek: Picard," it was revealed that Deanna would go on to name her own daughter Kestra in a tribute to her dearly departed sister.

How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.
  • World-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness.
  • When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.].

World-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he indicates he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he mentioned through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

In a recent development, but he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I said, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”.

So instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he remarked. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”.

Sources indicate that his 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” said Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”.

How’s his French? “Zero,” he remarked. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”.

According to recent reports, the filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” mentioned Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”.

In a recent development, when it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” said Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”.

Industry observers note that one serious matter for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he said. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”.

Recent findings suggest that of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he said. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”.

According to recent reports, the filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”.

And Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he remarked. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”.

Was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he remarked. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”.

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he remarked, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it was actually quite an exciting moment earlier this year when Bethesda finally broke cover to give us updates on basically everything they have going on right now. That meant that we finally know what's going on with Fallout, The Elder Scrolls, and even Starfield, if anyone is still invested in how that plays out in the future.

For Fallout in particular, we got a ton of exciting information, including confirmation that both Fallout 3 and Fallout: Latest Vegas were getting the remakes that had been rumored for a long time. In addition, Fallout 5 was also confirmed to be entering full development, though given the protracted cycles of AAA games, the crushing reality is that it's likely still a long way away from being made available to players.

Though things have been relatively quiet since, there has now been an update and it further cements exactly what we though the situation was going to be.

As first reported by GameRant, Bethesda has now reiterated to fans that Fallout 5 remains their "long-term destination," and it will likely be the last of the previously declared projects to arrive in our laps.

According to recent reports, the story of Fallout 5 up to this point has been one of frustratingly little progress, particularly given how major the studio is. Todd Howard first spoke about the game all the way back in 2018 (now known as the cursed year), when he simply confirmed that it would be a single-player effort. He then went on to confirm that they had a one-pager for the game in 2021, before he confirmed a year later that it would be their next big project after The Elder Scrolls VI.

Sources indicate that back then, there would have been plenty of players out there who were expecting to be playing The Elder Scrolls VI by now, but that obviously isn't the case. In fact, it would be a major surprise if we are playing it before 2028, which likely means that Fallout 5 is going to be considerably further away, well into the 2030s.

The only potential silver lining to that timeline is that new Xbox head Asha Sharma has made it very clear that she wants Fallout to be at the center of the company's strategy moving forward. Possibly motivated by the success of the Prime Video adaptation, it may well be that additional resources are moved across to get the game out sooner.

It has been revealed that at the same time, those remakes we mentioned earlier should also be along much sooner than that, allowing us to explore two of the better RPGs of all-time in brand-latest fidelity. Though we don't have dates just yet, 2027 does seem like a reasonable estimate for the first of those, finally giving us something to do with the franchise while we wait.

Even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a newly introduced popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

It has been revealed that one of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

Industry observers note that “With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler said. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”.

But while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

“When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he mentioned. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump said.
  • Trump mentioned Georgia and Latest Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump said his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump said. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

Trump mentioned Georgia and Latest Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he said, “Hollywood would open again.”.

Trump said his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

The bill’s sponsors confirmed more than 60 new House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he said, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”.

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

“Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she stated in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”.

Industry observers note that A floor vote has yet to be unveiled, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

For crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s latest Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff said.

#51295. Tech Report: 5 Thriller Movies We Actually Want To See a Remake Of

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1396 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Collider ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: 5 Thriller Movies We Actually Want To See a Remake Of

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1396 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Feel free to connect with him or check out his work.
  • Remakes have a bad reputation, and unfortunately, most of the time, they have earned it.
  • Recent findings suggest that A straight copy of a classic thriller has almost no suspense left to offer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

Remakes have a bad reputation, and unfortunately, most of the time, they have earned it. The problem is that studios love banking on famous titles and hoping nostalgia will do the heavy lifting. That doesn’t really work with the thriller genre, where the whole experience depends on not knowing what happens next. Once audiences know the twist, there is very little reason to sit through the same story again.

Recent findings suggest that A straight copy of a classic thriller has almost no suspense left to offer. This means that the thrillers that are actually worth remaking are a little different. They’re the ones with brilliant setups that were either held back by their era or were way ahead of their time, with their fears feeling more real today than ever before. Here is a list of five thriller movies people actually want to see remade, as long as they have the right filmmakers behind them.

Industry observers note that dead Calm is a thriller that only needs three people and a lot of open water. The film follows Nicole Kidman and Sam Neill as Rae and John Ingram, a married couple who set out on a long sailing trip across the Pacific to grieve after their young son is killed in a car accident. Out in the middle of nowhere, they spot a man named Hughie (Billy Zane) frantically rowing away from a sinking ship. Hughie claims that the rest of his crew died of food poisoning, but when John rows over to investigate, the bodies he discovers tell a very different story. By then, Hughie has taken off in the couple’s yacht, and Rae is trapped aboard with him.

Recent findings suggest that the best thing about Dead Calm is how simple it is. The film is a cat-and-mouse game with nowhere to run and nobody coming to help. What’s even better is that director Phillip Noyce squeezes every bit of tension out of this narrative. That complexity makes it a natural fit for a modern remake. A upcoming version would just need to deal with the fact that satellite phones and GPS make getting stranded at sea much harder today, which could actually add an interesting twist to the story. All a Dead Calm remake needs is a smart director and two strong leads to become the kind of adrenaline-fueled, nerve-wracking thriller that has been missing from the significant screen for a while now.

Industry observers note that brian De Palma’s Blow Out bombed at the box office when it first came out, but it has since been recognized as one of the greatest conspiracy thrillers ever made. The film stars John Travolta as sound-effects technician Jack Terry, who works on cheap slasher movies. One night, while recording sounds in a park, Jack captures a car swerving off a bridge and into the river. He manages to rescue a young woman named Sally (Nancy Allen) from the wreck, but the man driving, a governor who was planning to run for president, is killed. When Jack plays back his tape, he hears something that sounds like a gunshot right before the tire blows out, and he soon realizes he has recorded a murder that powerful people want covered up.

Industry observers note that blow Out is a thriller story about how easily the truth can be buried, and that idea feels even more relevant now. In 1981, Jack’s audio tape was the only proof that something was wrong. A modern remake of the film could explore what happens when evidence can be faked, edited, or dismissed as a deepfake in seconds. Jack’s obsession with proving what he heard would hit even harder in a world where nobody knows what to believe anymore. The original’s devastating ending is also a significant part of why audiences rejected it back then, but it works perfectly today. Blow Out is a near-perfect film, but its central idea is begging to be updated for the age of misinformation.

Marathon Man is the movie that made an entire generation afraid of going to the dentist. The story follows history graduate Babe Levy (Dustin Hoffman), who spends his free time training for a marathon. His life is turned upside down when his older brother, Doc (Roy Scheider), turns out to be a secret government agent who has gotten tangled up with Dr. Christian Szell (Laurence Olivier), a Nazi war criminal hiding in South America. What’s worse is that Szell has come to New York to collect a fortune in stolen diamonds, and he is convinced that Babe knows something that could put them at risk. Marathon Man, written by William Goldman from his own novel, is famous for the scene where Szell tortures Babe with dental tools, along with the one where Holocaust survivors recognize him on the streets of New York’s diamond district.

Industry observers note that olivier’s menacing performance earned him an Oscar nomination for the role and practically defined the film. Hoffman also deserves his flowers for portraying Babe’s confusion with extreme conviction, which made the audience sympathize with him every step of the way. Nearly 50 years later, the idea of a war criminal hiding in plain sight, protected by money and powerful friends, still feels frighteningly relevant. Most younger viewers have never seen the original, though, and a fresh version could introduce them to one of the most unsettling stories the genre has ever produced.

The Parallax View is the ultimate paranoid thriller, and it might be even more unsettling today than it was in the 1970s. The film begins with the assassination of a U.S. senator at the top of Seattle’s Space Needle. Years later, reporter Joe Frady (Warren Beatty) notices that witnesses to the killing keep dying one after another. His investigation leads him to the Parallax Corporation, a shadowy company that seems to be recruiting troubled men and training them to become assassins.

In a recent development, the film, directed by Alan J. Pakula, who also made All the President’s Men, was released at a time when Americans had lost faith in the people in charge after a string of political assassinations and the Watergate scandal. Its most famous scene is a disturbing montage that Parallax uses to test its recruits, where people are shown flashing images of family and patriotism alongside violence until it’s hard to tell the difference. That idea of a company quietly searching for angry, lonely men to manipulate feels eerily close to how online radicalization works today. A remake could easily swap the old-fashioned test for social media algorithms, and it would be just as terrifying. Paramount+ revealed plans for a series version back in 2021, but there has been little news since, and The Parallax View is long overdue for an update.

Wait Until Dark features one of the scariest showdowns in movie history, and it’s the perfect candidate for a remake. The film, based on Frederick Knott’s play, stars Audrey Hepburn as Susy Hendrix, a woman who recently lost her sight and lives in a New York City apartment with her husband, Sam (Efrem Zimbalist Jr.). Without realizing it, Sam brings home a doll that has been stuffed with heroin, and a group of criminals led by the ruthless Roat (Alan Arkin) will do anything to get it back. They come up with an elaborate con to trick Susy into handing it over, but it turns out she is not one to underestimate.

The film’s climax is what most people remember it for. Susy realizes that if she can’t see, the best way to win is to make sure nobody else can either, and she smashes every light in the apartment. When the film first came out, some theaters even dimmed their lights to make the sequence feel even scarier. The problem is that much of the first half has aged poorly, since almost everyone around Susy treats her like a helpless child. A remake could keep the brilliant premise while giving Susy the strength and intelligence she deserves from the very first scene. Hepburn earned an Oscar nomination for the role, but Wait Until Dark is ready for a brand-latest heroine who can outsmart her attackers right from the start.
